issue reviews some of the performance gaps of the distance functions in  `scipy.spatial.distance`, and proposes a “plug-in” mechanism aimed at making it easier to address these gaps by delegating the core computation to “distance computation kernels”.

### Background

Performance (i.e. speed) has been a key consideration for implementing the distance functions (also referred to as “metrics”) in `scipy.spatial.distance`. The current approach is to implement the metrics in C++ and expose them to Python (using pybind11) via the [cdist](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.distance.cdist.html) and [pdist](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.distance.pdist.html) functions. The work in progress is tracked by the following issues and PRs:

- gh-13629 describes significant slowdown when a metric is coded purely in Python. This indicates a need for more efficient implementations.
- gh-14077 is a meta issue that tracks the migration from C to C++ to improve performance and flexibility.
- gh-14155 is an attempt to implement cosine distance in C++, but was stale due to performance regression.
- gh-18537 discusses native support for `bool` input for Boolean metrics. The current C++ implementation converts `bool` to `double`.
- gh-21263 is the latest PR to migrate the remaining metrics from C or Python to C++.

Performance is evaluated by a set of [benchmark tests](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/main/benchmarks/benchmarks/spatial.py). For each metric, four benchmarks are defined, each with three workload configurations:

- [cdist](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/c0065b69a98be549b46e44573bbf3c13e98681da/benchmarks/benchmarks/spatial.py#L378): 10x3 vs 10x3, 100x3 vs 100x3, 1000x3 vs 1000x3
- [pdist](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/c0065b69a98be549b46e44573bbf3c13e98681da/benchmarks/benchmarks/spatial.py#L384): 10x3, 100x3, 1000x3
- [weighted cdist](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/c0065b69a98be549b46e44573bbf3c13e98681da/benchmarks/benchmarks/spatial.py#L444): 10x3 vs 10x3, 20x3 vs 20x3, 100x3 vs 100x3
- [weighted pdist](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/c0065b69a98be549b46e44573bbf3c13e98681da/benchmarks/benchmarks/spatial.py#L449): 10x3, 20x3, 100x3

Note that all workloads cover exclusively vectors with three elements.

The benchmark results are shown on [this website](https://pv.github.io/scipy-bench/). Each benchmark is presented as a chart that plots its run-time (lower is better) over the history of commits. The charts confirm that the distance implementations have performance improved over time.

### Challenges

While the current C++ implementation achieves excellent performance for the types of workload it covers, there remain  scenarios where it falls short of expectation.

The main performance gap appears to be with large input. For example:

- gh-16023 reports suboptimal performance of `cdist('euclidean')` for `f32` input of size 3360x3072 vs 15904x3072. An alternative formula is suggested in the discussion, but it is prone to catastrophic cancellation and therefore [unlikely to be accepted](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/16023#issuecomment-1121168502) for SciPy.

- gh-12570 suggests an alternative formula to compute `cdist('mahanalobis')` faster for input of size 500x500 vs 500x500. However, this formula is prone to the same catastrophic cancellation problem and is therefore [unlikely to be accepted](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/12570#issuecomment-791041213) for SciPy.

- gh-11280 raises a requirement to compute distance for `f32` and `f16` input of length 60K. The original intent was to save memory, but it certainly has a speed impact too. `f32` is possible with the current C++ infrastructure (though not yet implemented). `f16` seems much more challenging to implement within the current infrastructure.

- gh-5657 discusses the general use of BLAS operations (dot product and matrix multiplication) for distance computations involving vectors of length 2K to 10K. The discussions seem to be inclusive with no clear action plan.

- gh-19454 introduces an SIMD-based library that boosts performance especially for lower-precision input. The benchmarks involve vectors of length 1536.

There are also performance issues raised for the Python metric implementations:

- gh-20147 reports performance degrade of `distance.mahanalobis` for input dimension above 100. It seems to be related to an upstream bug.

- gh-20561 and gh-20570 propose a micro-optimization for `distance.chebyshev` that improves speed for input vector over 40 dimensions.

- gh-12537, gh-6089 and gh-6088 ask for support of *broadcasted*, instead of *cross*, distance. They suggest to add an `axis` parameter to the Python implementations to take advantage of NumPy's vectorization.

While these issues are raised with the Python implementation, an implementation in C++ would likely be more performant, and would certainly reduce code duplication and potential inconsistencies.

### Alternatives

Some libraries provide specialized distance functions that improve the performance for certain workloads.

[sklearn.metrics](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/api/sklearn.metrics.html) provides specialized implementations for euclidean distance and cosine distance, among others. For [euclidean_distance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.pairwise.euclidean_distances.html) they employ a faster formula that saves a constant proportion of instructions and takes advantage of BLAS matrix multiplication for cross distance. The caveat is that the formula is prone to catastrophic cancellation for inputs that varies wildly in scale. For [cosine_similarity](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine_similarity.html) they use BLAS matrix multiplication for cross distance after normalizing the inputs. The limitation is that the technique can’t readily be applied to pdist type of query.

[MATLAB’s pdist function](https://www.mathworks.com/help/stats/pdist.html) provides the “fasteuclidean” metric as an alternative to “euclidean”. It computes the Euclidean distance in the same way that sklearn does, and therefore shares the same caveat described above.

[SimSIMD](https://github.com/ashvardanian/SimSIMD) provides SIMD-accelerated vector-vector distance implementations of Euclidean, cosine, and a few other metrics, for various data types including f16 and bf16. Cross distance computation is implemented by double looping.

Compared to the above alternatives, SciPy offers a few advantages:

- A wider selection of metrics
- Support for weighted metric
- Better numerical accuracy
- Versatile interface (cdist, pdist, vector-vector)

Given SciPy’s rich features, it seems impractical for an alternative to fully substitute SciPy’s implementation. Likewise, it seems impractical for SciPy’s implementation to suit all types of workloads, given the diverse requirements. It probably makes the most sense to combine the best of both — that is the idea of this proposal.

### Proposal

The goal is to enable the user to access specialized distance implementations via SciPy’s API, so that they can take advantage of SciPy’s rich ecosystem while at the same time fulfilling specific performance requirements for certain use cases.

To achieve this, I propose to split the core computation logic of a metric into “distance computation kernels” with one of the following signatures:

```C
typedef void InType;   // for exposition
typedef void OutType; // for exposition

// Compute the distance between two vectors
typedef int (*DistanceScalar)(
    const InType *x,  // input n-vector
    const InType *y,  // input n-vector
    size_t n,         // number of elements per vector
    OutType *out      // output scalar
);

// Compute the distance between corresponding row vectors in x and y
typedef int (*DistanceVector)(
    const InType *x,  // input m-by-n matrix (row major)
    const InType *y,  // input m-by-n matrix (row major)
    size_t n,         // number of elements per vector
    size_t m,         // number of vectors
    OutType *out      // output m-vector
);

// Compute the distance between every row vector of x versus every row vector of y
typedef int (*DistanceMatrix)(
    const InType *x,  // input mx-by-n matrix (row major)
    const InType *y,  // input my-by-n matrix (row major)
    size_t n,         // number of elements per vector
    size_t mx,        // number of vectors in x
    size_t my,        // number of vectors in y
    OutType *out      // output mx-by-my matrix (row major)
);
```

A kernel may also have one of the following “extended” signatures to support strided input/output and extra metric arguments (such as weight).

<details>

<summary>Extended signatures</summary>

```C
#define NUM_EXTRA 1     // for exposition only

typedef int (*DistanceScalarEx)(
    const InType *x,      // input n-vector
    const ssize_t xs[1], // stride of x (in number of elements)
    const InType *y,      // input n-vector
    const ssize_t ys[1], // stride of y (in number of elements)
    size_t n,             // number of elements per vector
    OutType *out    // output scalar
#if NUM_EXTRA >= 1
    , const OutType *arg1  // extra argument 1
    , const ssize_t *arg1s // stride of arg1 (in number of elements)
#endif
);

typedef int (*DistanceVectorEx)(
    const InType *x,      // input m-by-n matrix (row major)
    const ssize_t xs[2],   // strides of x (in number of elements)
    const InType *y,      // input m-by-n matrix (row major)
    const ssize_t ys[2],   // strides of y (in number of elements)
    size_t n,             // number of elements per vector
    size_t m,             // numbers of vectors
    const OutType *out,    // output m-vector
    const ssize_t outs[1]   // strides of y
#if NUM_EXTRA >= 1
    , const OutType *arg1  // extra argument 1
    , const ssize_t *arg1s // strides of arg1 (in number of elements)
#endif
);

typedef int (*DistanceMatrixEx)(
    const InType *x,       // input mx-by-n matrix (row major)
    const ssize_t xs[2],   // strides of x (in number of elements)
    const InType *y,       // input my-by-n matrix (row major)
    const ssize_t ys[2],   // strides of y (in number of elements)
    size_t n,              // number of elements per vector
    size_t mx,             // number of vectors in x
    size_t my,             // number of vectors in y,
    OutType *out,            // output mx-by-my matrix (row major)
    const ssize_t outs[2]  // strides of out
#if NUM_EXTRA >= 1
    , const OutType *arg1  // extra argument 1
    , const ssize_t *arg1s // stride of arg1 (in number of elements)
#endif
);
```

</details>

*Remark*. The caller must ensure that (1) the input, output, and extra arguments are properly aligned, (2) the byte stride is a multiple of the element size, and (3) the output buffer does not overlap with any other arguments (i.e. allowing all pointers to be “restrict” qualified).

A *backend* would provide kernel implementations (with the above signature) for combinations of metrics and data types. SciPy would serve as the *front-end* to transform a user call to one or more calls to the kernel, after performing preprocessing such as type promotion. To make kernels available for use by SciPy, the backend would first “register” itself by calling

```Python
backend_id = scipy.spatial.distance.add_distance_backend(backend_name)
```

to obtain a “backend_id”. (This id  may be used to “unregister” the backend.) Then it would register each kernel function it provides by calling

```Python
scipy.spatial.distance.add_distance_kernel(
    metric_spec: str,         # e.g. 'cosine.s', 'euclidean.v:', 'mahanalobis.m:w.m', 'minkowski.m:w.v:p.s'
    dtype_spec: str,       # e.g. 'f64', 'f32->f64'
    func: LowLevelCallable,   # wraps a C function pointer
    backend_name: str,  # identifies the backend
)
```

Here `metric` may include the name of extra arguments to be passed to the kernel, separated by colon. A standalone colon following the metric name indicates stride support. The shape of an extra argument is specified by the single letter `s` (scalar), `v` (contiguous n-vector), or `m` (contiguous, row-major n-by-n matrix). `in_dtype` specifies the type of `x` and `y`; `out_dtype` specifies the type of `out` as well as of the extra arguments.

SciPy would maintain a list of kernels for each (metric, in_dtype, out_dtype) combination. The stock implementations are registered at start-up. When distance computation is requested, the best-match kernel is used to perform the computation. If no match exists, SciPy would attempt type promotion and possibly other transforms to find a usable kernel.

For an end user to “activate” a specialized metric implementation, the minimum they have to do is to add one line anywhere before calling the distance function, e.g.

```Python
import fast_euclidean

...

d = cdist(x, y, 'euclidean') # as usual
```

This assumes that some `fast_euclidean` package installs a fast euclidean kernel for the “euclidean” metric upon module import. (Though not shown here, it is also possible to install metrics not recognized by SciPy.)

### Discussion

**How would the proposal help address the challenges listed above?**

If the user has a (performance or functional) requirement not satisfied by SciPy, they could install a custom backend with the desired performance / functionality and use it seamlessly with SciPy. No need to wait for SciPy’s implementation (which can take time) or resort to other packages (which can be tricky to integrate).

Broadcasted distance could be easily implemented by calling the PairedDistance kernel. (In fact, all the stock C++ metric implementations are essentially wrapping PairedDistance kernels.)

**How does the proposal interact with the existing distance computation infrastructure in SciPy?**

The existing implementation of SciPy remains largely intact, except that some refactoring would be needed to isolate the core distance computation code from input preprocessing.

I expect SciPy's stock implementations to continue to improve for general use.

**Is the proposed mechanism backward compatible?**

Yes, the proposal is fully backward compatible for users of SciPy.

### Request for comments

I’d love to hear your feedback on this proposal. Do you think it addresses a valid problem? Do you think the solution makes sense? Do you think it might attract interest to vendor a backend? Any thoughts about the technical details (such as the kernel signature)? All sorts of comments are welcome!

Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

In https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21700 there is discussion about factoring a base class for statistical distributions under the new framework. For such a base class to be fully generic, it would need to cover (mixtures of) continuous, discrete, and singular distributions. The Cantor distribution is a fun example of a singular distribution. What does this implement/fix? This adds a function that accepts an instance of `stats.rv_continuous` and returns a subclass of `stats.ContinuousDistribution`. The `ContinuousDistribution` uses overridden methods of the `rv_continuous` class where possible (e.g. `pdf`, `logpdf`) but uses its own generic method implementations (which are often faster and more accurate). As an example inspired by gh-18799: ```python3 from scipy import stats GH = stats.wrap_rv_continuous(stats.gausshyper, support=(0, 1)) X = stats.gausshyper(a=1.5, b=2.5, c=2, z=0) Y = GH(a=1.5, b=2.5, c=2, z=0) ``` `X` is a "frozen" distribution object representing the Gauss hypergeometric distribution and `Y` is a corresponding instance of a `ContinuousDistribution`. Since `gausshyper_gen` defines `_pdf`, the `pdf` methods of the two objects behave identically: ```python3 X.pdf(0.3), Y.pdf(0.3) # (np.float64(1.6337206456367985), np.float64(1.6337206456367985)) ``` but because `gausshyper_gen` does not define `_cdf`, `Y` will use the `ContinuousDistribution` framework to evaluate the CDF, which tends to be much faster and more accurate than the generic implementation in the `rv_continuous` framework.
```python3 import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy import stats import numpy as np from scipy import stats from scipy import special as sc from time import perf_counter from mpmath import mp mp.dps = 50 a, b, c, z = 1.5, 2.5, 2, 0 def _pdf_mpmath(x): a, b, c, z = 1.5, 2.5, 2, 0 a, b, c, z = mp.mpf(a), mp.mpf(b), mp.mpf(c), mp.mpf(z) Cinv = mp.gamma(a) * mp.gamma(b) / mp.gamma(a + b) * mp.hyp2f1(c, a, a + b, -z) return mp.one / Cinv * x ** (a - mp.one) * (mp.one - x) ** (b - mp.one) / (mp.one + z * x) ** c X = stats.gausshyper(a=a, b=b, c=c, z=z) GH = stats.wrap_rv_continuous(stats.gausshyper, (0, 1)) Y = GH(a=a, b=b, c=c, z=z) x = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)[1:] tic = perf_counter() cdf_vals = X.cdf(x) toc = perf_counter() t1 = toc-tic print(f"Time for 1000 CDF value (old): {t1}") tic = perf_counter() cdf_vals2 = Y.cdf(x) toc = perf_counter() t2 = toc-tic print(f"Time for 1000 CDF value (new): {t2}") cdf_vals3 = np.asarray([mp.quad(_pdf_mpmath, (mp.mpf(0), mp.mpf(xi))) for xi in x], dtype=np.float64) rerr = abs((cdf_vals - cdf_vals3)/(cdf_vals3)) rerr2 = abs((np.asarray(cdf_vals2) - cdf_vals3)/(cdf_vals3)) rerr = rerr[rerr != 0] rerr2 = rerr2[rerr2 != 0] print(f"Speedup: {t1/t2}") print(f"gmean of relative error (old): {stats.gmean(rerr)}") print(f"gmean of relative error (new): {stats.gmean(rerr2)}") print(f"max relative error (old): {np.max(rerr)}") print(f"max relative error (new): {np.max(rerr2)}") ```
``` Time for 1000 CDF value (main): 0.737669125024695 Time for 1000 CDF value (main): 0.006104291998781264 Speedup: 120.84433791371256 gmean of relative error (old): 8.034300408110537e-16 gmean of relative error (new): 4.553789318107634e-16 max relative error (old): 1.1235272457145405e-07 max relative error (new): 1.445515587446478e-13 ``` And we get all the bells and whistles of `ContinuousDistribution`: ```python3 (Y + 1).mode() # np.float64(1.2500000068559416) Y.plot() ``` #### Additional information Questions: - What should this be called? (Maybe see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21707#issuecomment-2412636465.) - Should it be public? I think so, because I don't think we want to create public versions of all old distributions with the new interface. Thoughts: - Not all distributions will "just work" as written because some call other private methods of `rv_continuous` I think I can work around this. - Currently, the user has to pass the support of the distribution as the second argument. (If they don't, they don't get a truncated distribution... just something that is wrong sometimes.) We could eliminate this need by defining it for all instances of `rv_continuous`. (The domain of the parameters is given by `_shape_info`.) - We could offer a public interface like this for creating custom distributions so users don't need to delve into the private methods of `ContinuousDistribution` to create their own distributions. Of course, there will be several other subclasses, like `DiscreteDistribution`, etc. Should that superclass be created in this PR or shall we do a separate PR and rebase this after that merges?~~ I'd like to add `_ProbabilityDistribution` in this PR. Thoughts: - There are many ways of making this more efficient at the cost of extra complexity. Let's keep this simple. - Currently this is only for distributions with scalar shapes (not arrays). Separate PR can extend to array shapes. - I remember a request for zero-inflated distributions. I'd like to enable this by creating a degenerate/Dirac continuous distribution in a follow-up PR. The obvious alternative is to wait until there is a discrete uniform distribution (which could have all its mass at zero). - When there are discrete distributions in the mixture, I suppose the PDF at the support values of the discrete distributions will be infinite? And perhaps this class should _also_ have a PMF method, and the PMF at values that are not in the support of a discrete distribution would be zero? - I'll probably want to test edge behavior with distributions that have finite support (but it doesn't really matter until these are public). - `mode` may not return the global maximum of the PDF. This is [already documented](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/generated/scipy.stats.Normal.mode.html#scipy.stats.Normal.mode). - See gh-21707, which would allow mixtures to be composed of most existing continuous distributions. Reference issue
Closes gh-21135.

#### What does this implement/fix?
As explained in gh-21135, the handling of degenerate input (such as empty input, zero input, or zero weights) for the Boolean metrics in `scipy.spatial.distance` varies across metrics / Python vs C++ / weighted vs unweighted.

Two previous PRs, gh-7373 and gh-13773, fixed the situation for `jaccard` and `yule`, respectively, by returning `0.0` in this case.

This PR fixes the other Boolean metrics (`hamming`, `dice`, `rogerstanimoto`, `russellrao`, `sokalsneath`) in the same way. I leave `kulczynski1` and `sokalmichener` unchanged since they are being deprecated (see gh-21572).

#### Additional information
This PR only deals with Boolean metrics (and does not touch real metrics) to limit the scope of impact.

gh-1403 address the issue for `sokalsneath` in a different way by raising `ValueError` in the Python implementation (and returning `nan` in the C++ implementation). Since `sokalsneath` is a monotone transform of `jaccard`, I think it would be more consistent to return `0.0` What does this implement/fix? This adds a function that accepts an instance of `stats.rv_continuous` and returns a subclass of `stats.ContinuousDistribution`. The `ContinuousDistribution` uses overridden methods of the `rv_continuous` class where possible (e.g. `pdf`, `logpdf`) but uses its own generic method implementations (which are often faster and more accurate). As an example inspired by gh-18799: ```python3 from scipy import stats GH = stats.wrap_rv_continuous(stats.gausshyper, support=(0, 1)) X = stats.gausshyper(a=1.5, b=2.5, c=2, z=0) Y = GH(a=1.5, b=2.5, c=2, z=0) ``` `X` is a "frozen" distribution object representing the Gauss hypergeometric distribution and `Y` is a corresponding instance of a `ContinuousDistribution`. Since `gausshyper_gen` defines `_pdf`, the `pdf` methods of the two objects behave identically: ```python3 X.pdf(0.3), Y.pdf(0.3) # (np.float64(1.6337206456367985), np.float64(1.6337206456367985)) ``` but because `gausshyper_gen` does not define `_cdf`, `Y` will use the `ContinuousDistribution` framework to evaluate the CDF, which tends to be much faster and more accurate than the generic implementation in the `rv_continuous` framework.
```python3 import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy import stats import numpy as np from scipy import stats from scipy import special as sc from time import perf_counter from mpmath import mp mp.dps = 50 a, b, c, z = 1.5, 2.5, 2, 0 def _pdf_mpmath(x): a, b, c, z = 1.5, 2.5, 2, 0 a, b, c, z = mp.mpf(a), mp.mpf(b), mp.mpf(c), mp.mpf(z) Cinv = mp.gamma(a) * mp.gamma(b) / mp.gamma(a + b) * mp.hyp2f1(c, a, a + b, -z) return mp.one / Cinv * x ** (a - mp.one) * (mp.one - x) ** (b - mp.one) / (mp.one + z * x) ** c X = stats.gausshyper(a=a, b=b, c=c, z=z) GH = stats.wrap_rv_continuous(stats.gausshyper, (0, 1)) Y = GH(a=a, b=b, c=c, z=z) x = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)[1:] tic = perf_counter() cdf_vals = X.cdf(x) toc = perf_counter() t1 = toc-tic print(f"Time for 1000 CDF value (old): {t1}") tic = perf_counter() cdf_vals2 = Y.cdf(x) toc = perf_counter() t2 = toc-tic print(f"Time for 1000 CDF value (new): {t2}") cdf_vals3 = np.asarray([mp.quad(_pdf_mpmath, (mp.mpf(0), mp.mpf(xi))) for xi in x], dtype=np.float64) rerr = abs((cdf_vals - cdf_vals3)/(cdf_vals3)) rerr2 = abs((np.asarray(cdf_vals2) - cdf_vals3)/(cdf_vals3)) rerr = rerr[rerr != 0] rerr2 = rerr2[rerr2 != 0] print(f"Speedup: {t1/t2}") print(f"gmean of relative error (old): {stats.gmean(rerr)}") print(f"gmean of relative error (new): {stats.gmean(rerr2)}") print(f"max relative error (old): {np.max(rerr)}") print(f"max relative error (new): {np.max(rerr2)}") ```
``` Time for 1000 CDF value (main): 0.737669125024695 Time for 1000 CDF value (main): 0.006104291998781264 Speedup: 120.84433791371256 gmean of relative error (old): 8.034300408110537e-16 gmean of relative error (new): 4.553789318107634e-16 max relative error (old): 1.1235272457145405e-07 max relative error (new): 1.445515587446478e-13 ``` And we get all the bells and whistles of `ContinuousDistribution`: ```python3 (Y + 1).mode() # np.float64(1.2500000068559416) Y.plot() ``` #### Additional information Questions: - ~~What should this be called? (Maybe see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21707#issuecomment-2412636465.)~~ We'll make it `ContinuousDistribution.from_rv_continuous`. - ~~Should it be public? I think so, because I don't think we want to create public versions of all old distributions with the new interface.~~ Yes. Thoughts: - Not all distributions will "just work" as written because some call other private methods of `rv_continuous` I think I can work around this. - Currently, the user has to pass the support of the distribution as the second argument. (If they don't, they don't get a truncated distribution... just something that is wrong sometimes.) We could eliminate this need by defining it for all instances of `rv_continuous`. (The domain of the parameters is given by `_shape_info`.) - We could offer a public interface like this for creating custom distributions so users don't need to delve into the private methods of `ContinuousDistribution` to create their own distributions. Should the random variables and their probabilities be separate lists (as they are now) or, say, a list of tuples?~~ People seem happy with separate `components` (positional only) and `weights`. - ~~To avoid copy-pasting all the method documentation, I was thinking that this and `ContinuousDistribution` should be a subclass of a new superclass `StatisticalDistribution`, and method documentation would go there. Of course, there will be several other subclasses, like `DiscreteDistribution`, etc. Should that superclass be created in this PR or shall we do a separate PR and rebase this after that merges?~~ I'd like to add `_ProbabilityDistribution` in this PR. Thoughts: - There are many ways of making this more efficient at the cost of extra complexity. Let's keep this simple. - Currently this is only for distributions with scalar shapes (not arrays). Separate PR can extend to array shapes. - I remember a request for zero-inflated distributions. I'd like to enable this by creating a degenerate/Dirac continuous distribution in a follow-up PR. The obvious alternative is to wait until there is a discrete uniform distribution (which could have all its mass at zero). - When there are discrete distributions in the mixture, I suppose the PDF at the support values of the discrete distributions will be infinite? And perhaps this class should _also_ have a PMF method, and the PMF at values that are not in the support of a discrete distribution would be zero? - I'll probably want to test edge behavior with distributions that have finite support (but it doesn't really matter until these are public). - `mode` may not return the global maximum of the PDF. This is [already documented](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/generated/scipy.stats.Normal.mode.html#scipy.stats.Normal.mode). - See gh-21707, which would allow mixtures to be composed of most existing continuous distributions. What does this implement/fix? This adds `scipy.stats.Mixture`, a class for mixture distributions. ```python3 import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy.stats import Mixture, Normal vars = (Normal(mu=-1.2, sigma=1.1), Normal(mu=1.3, sigma=0.9)) weights = (0.4, 0.6) X = Mixture(vars, weights=weights) x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 300) plt.plot(x, X.pdf(x)) plt.hist(X.sample(10000), density=True, bins=30) plt.show() ``` #### Additional information Questions: - ~~What should the class be called?~~ People seem happy with `Mixture`. - ~~What should the arguments be called? Should the random variables and their probabilities be separate lists (as they are now) or, say, a list of tuples?~~ People seem happy with separate `components` (positional only) and `weights`. - ~~To avoid copy-pasting all the method documentation, I was thinking that this and `ContinuousDistribution` should be a subclass of a new superclass `StatisticalDistribution`, and method documentation would go there. Of course, there will be several other subclasses, like `DiscreteDistribution`, etc. Should that superclass be created in this PR or shall we do a separate PR and rebase this after that merges?~~ I'd like to add `_ProbabilityDistribution` in this PR. Thoughts: - There are many ways of making this more efficient at the cost of extra complexity. Let's keep this simple. - Currently this is only for distributions with scalar shapes (not arrays). Separate PR can extend to array shapes. - I remember a request for zero-inflated distributions. I'd like to enable this by creating a degenerate/Dirac continuous distribution in a follow-up PR. The obvious alternative is to wait until there is a discrete uniform distribution (which could have all its mass at zero). - When there are discrete distributions in the mixture, I suppose the PDF at the support values of the discrete distributions will be infinite? And perhaps this class should _also_ have a PMF method, and the PMF at values that are not in the support of a discrete distribution would be zero? - I'll probably want to test edge behavior with distributions that have finite support (but it doesn't really matter until these are public). - `mode` may not return the global maximum of the PDF. This is [already documented](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/generated/scipy.stats.Normal.mode.html#scipy.stats.Normal.mode). - See gh-21707, which would allow mixtures to be composed of most existing continuous distributions. Of course, there will be several other subclasses, like `DiscreteDistribution`, etc. Should that superclass be created in this PR or shall we do a separate PR and rebase this after that merges?~~ I'd like to add `_ProbabilityDistribution` in this PR. Thoughts: - There are many ways of making this more efficient at the cost of extra complexity. Let's keep this simple. - Currently this is only for distributions with scalar shapes (not arrays). Separate PR can extend to array shapes. - I remember a request for zero-inflated distributions. I'd like to enable this by creating a degenerate/Dirac continuous distribution in a follow-up PR. The obvious alternative is to wait until there is a discrete uniform distribution (which could have all its mass at zero). - When there are discrete distributions in the mixture, I suppose the PDF at the support values of the discrete distributions will be infinite? And perhaps this class should _also_ have a PMF method, and the PMF at values that are not in the support of a discrete distribution would be zero? - I'll probably want to test edge behavior with distributions that have finite support (but it doesn't really matter until these are public). - `mode` may not return the global maximum of the PDF. This is [already documented](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/generated/scipy.stats.Normal.mode.html#scipy.stats.Normal.mode). - See gh-21707, which would allow mixtures to be composed of most existing continuous distributions. The obvious alternative is to wait until there is a discrete uniform distribution (which could have all its mass at zero). - When there are discrete distributions in the mixture, I suppose the PDF at the support values of the discrete distributions will be infinite? And perhaps this class should _also_ have a PMF method, and the PMF at values that are not in the support of a discrete distribution would be zero? - I'll probably want to test edge behavior with distributions that have finite support (but it doesn't really matter until these are public). - `mode` may not return the global maximum of the PDF. Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

In https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21700 there is discussion about factoring a base class for statistical distributions under the new framework. For such a base class to be fully generic, it would need to cover (mixtures of) continuous, discrete, and [singular distributions](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_distribution).

The [Cantor distribution](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_distribution) is a curious example of a singular distribution. Having such a class would help to test/verify the “completeness” of the infrastructure.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

Add a class, `scipy.stats.Cantor`, that represents the Cantor distribution. The class would be derived from a base class to be formed.

### Describe alternatives you've considered.

_No response_

### Additional context (e.g. screenshots, GIFs)

Less curious singular distributions exist in higher dimensions. For example, a bivariate normal distribution constructed from two perfectly correlated normal variables.

I’m not aware of any statistical application involving the Cantor distribution. So this enhancement proposal is more for fun. Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

In https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21700 there is discussion about factoring a base class for statistical distributions under the new framework. For such a base class to be fully generic, it would need to cover (mixtures of) continuous, discrete, and [singular distributions](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_distribution).

The [Cantor distribution](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_distribution) is a curious example of a singular distribution. Having such a class would help to test/verify the “completeness” of the infrastructure.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

Add a class, `scipy.stats.Cantor`, that represents the Cantor distribution. The class would be derived from a base class to be formed.

### Describe alternatives you've considered.

_No response_

### Additional context (e.g. screenshots, GIFs)

Less curious singular distributions exist in higher dimensions. For example, a bivariate normal distribution constructed from two perfectly correlated normal variables.

I’m not aware of any statistical application involving the Cantor distribution. So this enhancement proposal is more for fun. I’d say those are the fun part and in fact quite enlightening.

> It does not behave like any "usual" distribution, and I don't see any real life application for it. It will only confuse users who try out distributions without checking the math, and if they do they will just ignore it.

I agree there’s probably little practical use of the distribution. But I don’t think it would cause much confusion — the CDF plot of Cantor distribution looks just like any empirical distribution, so I don’t foresee anything special in *using* it. (Though there is clearly something special in *writing* it.)

> (AFAIR, the only time I learned about Cantor set was as counter example to some probability or measure theory definitions.)

Quite the opposite — it is a counter example of heuristic reasoning about probability distributions. It is well treated within the framework of probability theory, and that’s why I propose to use it as a “test case” to verify the “completeness” of our new distribution framework — if the framework is compatible with Cantor (I think it is or at least almost is), we can be fairly confident that the framework will be able to handle *any* probability distribution to ever occur.

> How would you define and compute the expectation of a function w.r.t. the Cantor distribution

The mathematical definition is standard and is the same as any other distribution:

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] := \int_{[0,1]} g(x) \mathrm{d} \mu
$$

where $\mu$ is the probability measure and the integral is understood to be a Lebesgue integral.

My intent is less about adding the Cantor distribution itself but more about making sure that the new statistical distribution infrastructure has enough flexibility to support a wide range of custom distributions. Of course such “generality” needs to carefully defined — not too specific to exclude valid use cases, and not too generic to offer no aid to the user. (The old rv_generic framework is too “specific” in this sense since it’s not possible to implement mixed discrete-continuous distribution without hackish “monkey patching”.)

I really like the initiative of the new infrastructure and I’m confident it will enable new possibilities that make `scipy.stats` better. I took the liberty to investigate the “boundary” of the new infrastructure — what kind of distributions are possible to implement under the new framework, without hacking the framework itself? (It seems mixed discrete-continuous distributions are already under the radar of @mdhaber, which is great.)

After much research I arrived at the conclusion that the new infrastructure is really close to, if not yet, supporting *arbitrary* (univariate) probability distributions. I think this is an important point because it implies we will never have to invent a new new framework ever again due to the new framework lacking some feature that cannot be added in a backward compatible way.

How to ensure that generality is not compromised while defining/implementing methods of the new base class (say `_ProbabilityDistribution`)? I think the easiest way is to actually *have* a distribution that relies on the generality being available. If you don’t have a mixed discrete-continuous distribution, you won’t find out something doesn’t work for mixed discrete-continuous distribution. Likewise, if you don’t have a “weird” distribution like Cantor, you won’t know some specification/implementation doesn’t generalize to “weird” distributions.

An alternative to this generality is to state that the new infrastructure only supports mixture of discrete and continuous distributions. I think that will satisfy most practical applications, so is a viable choice. However, I’d still like to advocate for full generality because there is little extra coding effort to spend (if any at all) to go from mixed discrete-continuous to fully general, so why not? If the design is fully general, then it will never have to be revisited again. This probably saves resource in the long run.

I understand the above might be too “forward looking” and lacks traction probably because there’re not yet concrete examples to illustrate the loss of generality (apart from  mixed discrete-continuous distributions which are on the radar). It could have been more intuitively explained if concrete examples are gathered.

Therefore I’m closing this issue right now and we could possibly revisit when specific issues arise. Anyway I hope you could give a thought about singular distribution support when making specifications/implementations.

Thanks for your input!","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/scipy/scipy/issues/comments/2421266244/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"performed_via_github_app":null}}

Reference issue
Closes gh-21453

#### What does this implement/fix?
This adds a function that computes the $\xi$ correlation coefficient and performs an (asymptotic or permutation) test of independence.

#### Additional information
- `alternative` could be added, but two-sided and `alternative='less'` test seem unlikely to be useful
- It's arguable that ties should be automatically detected by using `_rankdata`, and this should inform the choice of statistic calculation method.  However, the p-value calculation is supposed to be based on whether the distribution underlying `y` is continuous or not - not whether there actually *are* ties. So it seems like we should be able to use `y_continuous` for both. Perhaps automatic detection (and maybe a `metod='auto'`) can be added in a follow -up.
- When there are ties in `x`, they are broken at random (an option suggested by the paper). Perhaps we can do something smarter in a follow-up, but let's leave it alone for now.
- `too_small=1` doesn't seem to be working for multidimensional arrays
- Should we document this as the $\xi$ statistic (using the Greek letter)?

#### What does this implement/fix?
This adds a function that computes the $\xi$ correlation coefficient and performs an (asymptotic or permutation) test of independence.

#### Additional information
- `alternative` could be added, but two-sided and `alternative='less'` test seem unlikely to be useful
- It's arguable that ties should be automatically detected by using `_rankdata`, and this should inform the choice of statistic calculation method.  However, the p-value calculation is supposed to be based on whether the distribution underlying `y` is continuous or not - not whether there actually *are* ties. So it seems like we should be able to use `y_continuous` for both. Perhaps automatic detection (and maybe a `metod='auto'`) can be added in a follow -up.
- When there are ties in `x`, they are broken at random (an option suggested by the paper). Perhaps we can do something smarter in a follow-up, but let's leave it alone for now.
- `too_small=1` doesn't seem to be working for multidimensional arrays
- Should we document this as the $\xi$ statistic (using the Greek letter)?

+import numpy as np
+from scipy import stats
+from scipy.stats._stats_py import _SimpleNormal, SignificanceResult, _get_pvalue
+from scipy.stats._axis_nan_policy import _axis_nan_policy_factory
+
+
+__all__ = ['xi_correlation']
+
+
+# TODO:

+def _xi_statistic(x, y, y_continuous):
+    # Compute xi correlation statistic
+
+    # `axis=-1` is guaranteed by _axis_nan_policy decorator
+    n = x.shape[-1]
+
+    # "Rearrange the data as (X(1), Y(1)), . . . ,(X(n), Y(n))
+    # such that X(1) ≤ ··· ≤ X(n)"
+    j = np.argsort(x, axis=-1)
+    j, y = np.broadcast_arrays(j, y)
+    y = np.take_along_axis(y, j, axis=-1)
+
+    # "Let ri be the rank of Y(i), that is, the number of j such that Y(j) ≤ Y(i)"
+    r = stats.rankdata(y, method='max', axis=-1)
+    # " additionally define li to be the number of j such that Y(j) ≥ Y(i)"
+    # Could probably compute this from r, but that can be an enhancement
+    l = stats.rankdata(-y, method='max', axis=-1)
+
+    num = np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(r, axis=-1)), axis=-1)
+    if y_continuous:  # [1] Eq. 1.1
+        statistic = 1 - 3 * num / (n ** 2 - 1)
+    else:  # [1] Eq. 1.2
+        den = 2 * np.sum((n - l) * l, axis=-1)
+        statistic = 1 - n * num / den
+
+    return statistic, r, l
+
+
+def _xi_std(r, l, y_continuous):
+    # Compute standard deviation of xi under null hypothesis of independence
+
+    # `axis=-1` is guaranteed by _axis_nan_policy decorator
+    n = np.float64(r.shape[-1])
+
+    # "Suppose that X and Y are independent and Y is continuous. Then
+    # √n·ξn(X, Y) → N(0, 2/5) in distribution as n → ∞"
+    if y_continuous:  # [1] Theorem 2.1
+        return np.sqrt(2 / 5) / np.sqrt(n)
+
+    # "Suppose that X and Y are independent. Then √n·ξn(X, Y)
+    # converges to N(0, τ²) in distribution as n → ∞
+    # [1] Eq. 2.2 and surrounding math
+    i = np.arange(1, n + 1)
+    u = np.sort(r, axis=-1)
+    v = np.cumsum(u, axis=-1)
+    an = 1 / n**4 * np.sum((2*n - 2*i + 1) * u**2, axis=-1)
+    bn = 1 / n**5 * np.sum((v + (n - i)*u)**2, axis=-1)
+    cn = 1 / n**3 * np.sum((2*n - 2*i + 1) * u, axis=-1)
+    dn = 1 / n**3 * np.sum((l * (n - l)), axis=-1)
+    tau = (an - 2*bn + cn**2) / dn**2
+
+    return np.sqrt(tau) / np.sqrt(n)
+
+
+def _xi_correlation_iv(y_continuous, method):
+    # Input validation for `xi_correlation`
+    # x, y, `axis` input validation taken care of by decorator
+
+    if y_continuous not in {True, False}:
+        raise ValueError('`y_continuous` must be boolean.')
+
+    if not isinstance(method, stats.PermutationMethod):
+        method = method.lower()
+        message = "`method` must be 'asymptotic' or a `PermutationMethod` instance."
+        if method != 'asymptotic':
+            raise ValueError(message)
+
+    return y_continuous, method
+
+
+def _unpack(res):
+    return res.statistic, res.pvalue

+def _xi_statistic(x, y, y_continuous):

+
+    # `axis=-1` is guaranteed by _axis_nan_policy decorator

+    y = np.take_along_axis(y, j, axis=-1)

+    # "Let ri be the rank of Y(i), that is, the number of j such that Y(j) ≤ Y(i)"

+        statistic = 1 - 3 * num / (n ** 2 - 1)
+    else:  # [1] Eq. 1.2
+        den = 2 * np.sum((n - l) * l, axis=-1)
+        statistic = 1 - n * num / den

+    return statistic, r, l
+
+
+def _xi_std(r, l, y_continuous):

+
+    # `axis=-1` is guaranteed by _axis_nan_policy decorator
+    n = np.float64(r.shape[-1])

+    # √n·ξn(X, Y) → N(0, 2/5) in distribution as n → ∞"
+    if y_continuous:  # [1] Theorem 2.1

Reference issue
Closes gh-21453

#### What does this implement/fix?
This adds a function that computes the $\xi$ correlation coefficient and performs an (asymptotic or permutation) test of independence.

#### Additional information
- `alternative` could be added, but two-sided and `alternative='less'` test seem unlikely to be useful
- It's arguable that ties should be automatically detected by using `_rankdata`, and this should inform the choice of statistic calculation method.  However, the p-value calculation is supposed to be based on whether the distribution underlying `y` is continuous or not - not whether there actually *are* ties. So it seems like we should be able to use `y_continuous` for both. Perhaps automatic detection (and maybe a `metod='auto'`) can be added in a follow -up.
- When there are ties in `x`, they are broken at random (an option suggested by the paper). Perhaps we can do something smarter in a follow-up, but let's leave it alone for now.
- `too_small=1` doesn't seem to be working for multidimensional arrays
- Should we document this as the $\xi$ statistic (using the Greek letter)?

#### What does this implement/fix?
This adds a function that computes the $\xi$ correlation coefficient and performs an (asymptotic or permutation) test of independence.

#### Additional information
- `alternative` could be added, but two-sided and `alternative='less'` test seem unlikely to be useful
- It's arguable that ties should be automatically detected by using `_rankdata`, and this should inform the choice of statistic calculation method.  However, the p-value calculation is supposed to be based on whether the distribution underlying `y` is continuous or not - not whether there actually *are* ties. So it seems like we should be able to use `y_continuous` for both. Perhaps automatic detection (and maybe a `metod='auto'`) can be added in a follow -up.
- When there are ties in `x`, they are broken at random (an option suggested by the paper). Perhaps we can do something smarter in a follow-up, but let's leave it alone for now.
- `too_small=1` doesn't seem to be working for multidimensional arrays
- Should we document this as the $\xi$ statistic (using the Greek letter)?

Closes gh-21453

#### What does this implement/fix?
This adds a function that computes the $\xi$ correlation coefficient and performs an (asymptotic or permutation) test of independence.

#### Additional information
- `alternative` could be added, but two-sided and `alternative='less'` test seem unlikely to be useful
- It's arguable that ties should be automatically detected by using `_rankdata`, and this should inform the choice of statistic calculation method.  However, the p-value calculation is supposed to be based on whether the distribution underlying `y` is continuous or not - not whether there actually *are* ties. So it seems like we should be able to use `y_continuous` for both. Perhaps automatic detection (and maybe a `metod='auto'`) can be added in a follow -up.
- When there are ties in `x`, they are broken at random (an option suggested by the paper). Perhaps we can do something smarter in a follow-up, but let's leave it alone for now.
- `too_small=1` doesn't seem to be working for multidimensional arrays
- Should we document this as the $\xi$ statistic (using the Greek letter)?

Reference issue
Closes gh-21453

#### What does this implement/fix?
This adds a function that computes the $\xi$ correlation coefficient and performs an (asymptotic or permutation) test of independence.

#### Additional information
- `alternative` could be added, but two-sided and `alternative='less'` test seem unlikely to be useful
- It's arguable that ties should be automatically detected by using `_rankdata`, and this should inform the choice of statistic calculation method.  However, the p-value calculation is supposed to be based on whether the distribution underlying `y` is continuous or not - not whether there actually *are* ties. So it seems like we should be able to use `y_continuous` for both. Perhaps automatic detection (and maybe a `metod='auto'`) can be added in a follow -up.
- When there are ties in `x`, they are broken at random (an option suggested by the paper). Perhaps we can do something smarter in a follow-up, but let's leave it alone for now.
- `too_small=1` doesn't seem to be working for multidimensional arrays
- Should we document this as the $\xi$ statistic (using the Greek letter)?

Reference issue
Closes gh-21135.

#### What does this implement/fix?
As explained in gh-21135, the handling of degenerate input (such as empty input, zero input, or zero weights) for the Boolean metrics in `scipy.spatial.distance` varies across metrics / Python vs C++ / weighted vs unweighted.

Two previous PRs, gh-7373 and gh-13773, fixed the situation for `jaccard` and `yule`, respectively, by returning `0.0` in this case.

This PR fixes the other Boolean metrics (`hamming`, `dice`, `rogerstanimoto`, `russellrao`, `sokalsneath`) in the same way. I leave `kulczynski1` and `sokalmichener` unchanged since they are being deprecated (see gh-21572).

#### Additional information
This PR only deals with Boolean metrics (and does not touch real metrics) to limit the scope of impact.

Discussion","color":"fef2c0","default":false,"description":null},{"id":16917467,"node_id":"MDU6TGFiZWwxNjkxNzQ2Nw==","url":"https://api.github.com/repos/numpy/numpy/labels/component:%20numpy.ma","name":"component: numpy.ma","color":"009800","default":false,"description":"masked arrays"}],"state":"open","locked":false,"assignee":null,"assignees":[],"milestone":null,"comments":3,"created_at":"2024-10-18T13:51:16Z","updated_at":"2024-10-21T00:03:42Z","closed_at":null,"author_association":"NONE","active_lock_reason":null,"body":"While reading the code and addressing some bugs related to `numpy/ma`, I encountered a few questions:

1. **Filling Values in Masked Arrays**:  
   Do we actually care about the exact fill value in masked arrays, given that they are masked by other values? If not, I believe I can resolve [bug 27580](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/27580) by simply removing the check for `inf`.

2. **Default Fill Value for Masked Arrays**:  
   Currently, the default fill value for masked arrays is defined by [`default_filler`](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/bdc8d4e03181deac5280166aec4188318050570d/numpy/ma/core.py#L167C1-L183C63) for Python data types. However, Python doesn’t have unsigned integer types, so for `np.uint` arrays, the default fill value is stored as `np.int64(999999)`. This causes issues in operations like `copyto(..., casting='samekind')`, as seen in [bug 27580](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/27580) and [bug 27269](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/27269). Should we consider using NumPy data types for the default fill value to ensure that the fill value matches the data type of the array (e.g., using a fill value that corresponds to integers or unsigned integers as appropriate)?

3. **Large Default Fill Values**:  
   Some default fill values seem quite large, such as `999999` for `np.int8` and `1.e20` for `np.float16`. What would be an appropriate default fill value for masked arrays, particularly for small data types like `int8` and `float16`? ([bug25677](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/25677))

4. **Reviewing `copyto` in Masked Arrays**:  
   Should we perform a comprehensive review of `copyto` functionality for masked arrays? It seems likely that similar bugs could exist due to the same root cause.

5. **Testing for Small Data Types**:  
   Should we extend the test suite to include small data types (e.g., `int8` and `float16`) to ensure that functions handle these cases correctly?

6. **Checking Method Consistency**
   Should we check the consistency of method between (no-masked) `masked array` and `ndarray`? There is some difference between methods and behaviors of (no-masked) `masked array` and `ndarray`, for example, see [bug27258](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/27258).

7. **Making Standard Clear**
   Some methods' standard is not clear. For example, should we auto mask the invalid result? In some function (such as `sqrt` , `std`) it does, but in other function (such as `median`, `mean`). Something more worse is that in the document some function don't mention it but auto change the mask (`sqrt` [`std`](https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/generated/numpy.ma.masked_array.std.html#numpy.ma.masked_array.std)) , and others do mention it but not change ([`mean`](https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/generated/numpy.ma.mean.html#numpy.ma.mean)).
   And something more worse is that, some important methods don't have clear explanation both in document and doc string, some of them are really important. For example, `__array_wrap__` , most of the callings to ufunc call it, and I think it might be the cause of the [bug25635](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/25635).

Since I'm not sure where to place these questions, I’ve marked this as a discussion for now.

For the particular case of `det`, I find two points that might be worth discussion:

First, it might not be a great choice to use `det` to test singularity. Consider the determinant of an $n \times n$ diagonal matrix with $a$ along the diagonal. Its determinant is $a^n$. If $a$ is small and $n$ is large, this can get arbitrarily small, and “effectively zero” by the `np.isclose` test. However, the matrix is clearly not singular. (A better way to test for singularity is to call `np.linalg.matrix_rank`.)

Secondly, it is somewhat tricky to use `np.isclose` to check for floating point equality, especially with the default tolerance parameters (rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8). In fact, the doc of np.isclose contains a section to alert about the default tolerance parameters. (Discussed in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/23912#discussion_r1365994920)

The function `np.clip` arguably has surprising casting behaviour:
```
a = np.arange(5, dtype='u1')
np.clip(a, -1, 3)
# OverflowError with NEP 50
np.clip(a, np.int64(-1), np.int64(3))
# array([0, 1, 2, 3, 3])  
# int64 dtype with NEP 50
# (before NEP 50, both examples gave int16)
```
I would naively have expected for the output dtype to always be the same as the input one. That this does not happen is because internally `np.clip` calls a ufunc: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/d885b0b546cbe2ab8401622c8d4db984ec5ea31b/numpy/_core/_methods.py#L92-L101
and these treat the arguments symmetrically.

It is possible to get the output dtype by setting `out` or `dtype`, but in the current implementation that still gives either the `OverflowError` or casting errors:
```
np.clip(a, np.int64(-1), np.int64(3), out=a)  # or dtype=a.dtype
# UFuncTypeError: Cannot cast ufunc 'clip' output from dtype('int64') to dtype('uint8') with casting rule 'same_kind'
```
adding `casting="unsafe"` gives the wrong answer, because `-1` becomes `255`.

I think it should be possible to make the `np.clip` function (probably not the `ufunc`) cast the `min` and `max` to `a.dtype`, but ensure that the valid ranges are respected (i.e., negative integers would become 0 if the dtype is unsigned). This would be similar to what was done in #24915, i.e., ideally we have the behaviour of `np.clip` be identical to
```
min = -1
max = 3
out = a.copy()
out[a<min] = min
out[a>max] = max
return out
```
(which still gives an out-of-bound error for `min=-1` because of `__setitem__`, but works for `min=np.int64(-1)`)

But perhaps this is more work than is warranted.

> Let T be the data type of x. >
> In math notation, this becomes
>
> $$
> \mathrm{clip}(x,a,b):= {\arg\min}_{ t \in T\cap [a,b]} | t-x |
> $$

The function `np.clip` arguably has surprising casting behaviour:
```

out[a>max] = max

```

I see the same symptoms as in #19563, but @rgommers said that it's unrelated, so here is a separate, more complete description.

I use the current Debian “testing” distribution, with the following system packages (current versions):
```
python3  3.11.8-1
python3.11  3.11.9-1
python3-virtualenv  20.26.2+ds-1
python3-pip-whl  24.1+dfsg-1
python3-setuptools  68.1.2-2
```
A fresh virtual environment created by `virtualenv` has the following:
```
Package    Version
---------- -------
pip        24.1
setuptools 68.1.2
wheel      0.43.0
```
Then I follow the [Building from source](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/building/index.html) instructions, installing everything else inside the virtual environment using its `pip`, and do `dev.py build`, which succeeds (besides some Fortran warnings). However, trying to run `dev.py build` again or `dev.py python` fails with an error message
```
RuntimeError: Can't install in non-empty directory: '<...>/build-install'
```

Examining what happens in `dev.py`, I've found that the actual install is made to
```
.../build-install/lib/python3/dist-packages
```
but [`get_site_packages()`](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/3959e8b28a8fdf9f6803fe34bf8f0e34909d840d/dev.py#L328C9-L328C26) trying to find it later gives instead
```
.../build-install/lib/python3.11/site-packages
```
Notice the `dist`/`site` difference (mentioned in the `get_site_packages()` docstring) and the generic `3` instead of specific `3.11` (not mentioned anywhere). Manually creating symlinks between the expected and actual locations seems to produce a usable installation. So it appears that different parts of `dev.py` (or the tools that it uses) construct the installation path by different means, which are not consistent.

This part that is supposed to treat Debian as a special case:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/3959e8b28a8fdf9f6803fe34bf8f0e34909d840d/dev.py#L342
actually is not executed because in my case there is no `'deb_system'` in `INSTALL_SCHEMES` (I don't know what is supposed to set it). Manually replacing this condition by `True` also seems to make the installation usable but produces several `Please avoid running ``setup.py`` directly.` warnings.

For comparison, the virtual environment itself has its packages in its `lib/python3.11/site-packages`, more consistent with what `get_site_packages()` currently thinks (without `'deb_system'`) rather than the structure currently created inside SciPy's `build-install`.

P.S. With the paths corrected as described above, I see that even if no files were changed, running `dev.py build` or `dev.py python` redoes a complete installation every time. Is this intentional (why?), or there is something else failing to recognize that the installed files are already up-to-date?

#### What does this implement/fix?
SciPy distributions like `lognorm`, `loglaplace`, and `loguniform` are examples of distributions underlying random variables whose logarithm is distributed according to a more fundamental distribution. To generalize this idea and avoid naming inconsistencies[^1], this PR adds a class that represents the distribution underlying a strictly increasing function of a random variable, and a funtion `exp` that takes the exponential of a random variable. For example, if `X = stats.Normal()`, `Y = exp(X)` is lognormally distributed.

#### Additional information

Or make these static methods (or methods?) of a superclass `ProbabilityDistribution`?

b. transform of a distribution
c. transform of a distribution family

Reference issue
Toward gh-20253.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Adds a private function `_iv_ratio_c` to compute `1-iv(v,x)/iv(v-1,x)` for `v >= 1` and `x >= 0`. One of `v` or `x` may be `inf` but not both.

This is complementary to `_iv_ratio` (gh-20457) but offers better accuracy for large `x`, where `_iv_ratio(v,x)` is close to 1.

The purpose of this function is to be used to compute the inverse of `_iv_ratio` using a univariate root finder accurately when the function value is close to 1. Preliminary results show that this helps to reduce the relative error (of the inverse) from a few hundred machine epsilon to a few machine epsilon.

#### Algorithm
Following the lines of gh-20457, let $R_\nu(x) := I_\nu(x) / I_{\nu-1}(x)$ for $\nu \ge 0.5$ and $x > 0$. We make use of the Perron continued fraction

$$
R_\nu(x) = \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

where $\gamma \in \mathbb R$ is an arbitrary constant and

$$
f(\nu,\gamma;x) = (2\nu -\gamma ) + \frac{-(2\nu+1)x}{2(\nu+x)+1+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+3)x}{2(\nu+x)+2+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+5)x}{2(\nu+x)+3+{}} \cdots
$$

The desired result is

$$
1-R_\nu(x) =\frac{\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

It is shown that the sequence of convergents, $(f_n)_{n=0}^\infty$, monotonically decreases toward $f$, and that

$$
\nu-0.5 <  \gamma+ f < \gamma+ f_n < 2\nu
$$

for all $n \ge 1$. The continued fraction $f$ is evaluated by $f_n$ for some $n \ge 1$ such that $|f_n-f_{n-1}| \le \epsilon |f_n|$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a given tolerance. The desired result is then evaluated by

$$
1-R_{\nu,n}(x) := \frac{\gamma+f_n}{x+\gamma+f_n}
$$

**Truncation error**.  When $1-R_\nu(x)$ is evaluated by $1-R_{\nu,n}(x)$, the relative truncation error is

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right|= \frac{x(f_n-f)}{(x+\gamma+f_n)(\gamma+f)}
$$

When the termination condition is satisfied, it is shown that

$$
\begin{align*}
f_n-f \le \epsilon | f_n| \frac{x}{2\nu-0.5}
\end{align*}
$$

(Note that the above bound is very coarse for large $x$.) Together with the fact that

$$
\frac{x}{x+\gamma+f_n} < \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f}=R
$$

and that

$$
\frac{1}{\gamma+f}=\frac{R}{x(1-R)},
$$

the relative truncation error may be bounded by

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right| < \frac{R^2}{1-R}\frac{\epsilon |f_n|}{2\nu-0.5}
$$

This bound can grow arbitrarily large as $R \rightarrow 1$, unless $f_n$ converges to $0$ “fast enough”. Thus, unlike `_iv_ratio`, the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` is not guaranteed even if infinite precision arithmetic were used. We proceed to test the accuracy numerically.

**Accuracy**. We test the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` numerically for each choice of $\gamma \in \\{0, \nu-0.5, 1.5\nu-0.15, 2\nu\\}$ and for various choices of $\epsilon$. For each $\gamma$ and $\epsilon$, a few values of $\nu$ are tested; for each $\nu$, 100,000 values of $x$ are chosen such that $R_\nu(x)$ is "approximately" evenly spaced over $(0,1)$. The computed result is then compared against reference values produced by `mpmath`.

The results show that the choice $\gamma=0$ consistently produces the smallest relative error. The accuracy improves with smaller $\epsilon$ but "flattens" after $2^{-56}$  Therefore, we choose $\gamma=0$ and $\epsilon=2^{-56}$ in this PR.

**Asymptotic expansion**

From the asymptotic expansion of modified Bessel functions (NIST, 10.40.1, 10.17.1)

$$
I_\nu(z) =\frac{e^z}{\sqrt{2\pi z}} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\left(\frac12 -\nu\right)_k \left(\frac12+\nu\right)_k }{ 2^k k!} z^{-k}
%(-1)^k a_k(\nu) z^{-k}
$$

where

$$
(a)\_k := \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (a+i)
$$

$$

$$

$$

Reference issue
Toward gh-20253.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Adds a private function `_iv_ratio_c` to compute `1-iv(v,x)/iv(v-1,x)` for `v >= 1` and `x >= 0`. One of `v` or `x` may be `inf` but not both.

This is complementary to `_iv_ratio` (gh-20457) but offers better accuracy for large `x`, where `_iv_ratio(v,x)` is close to 1.

The purpose of this function is to be used to compute the inverse of `_iv_ratio` using a univariate root finder accurately when the function value is close to 1. Preliminary results show that this helps to reduce the relative error (of the inverse) from a few hundred machine epsilon to a few machine epsilon.

#### Algorithm
Following the lines of gh-20457, let $R_\nu(x) := I_\nu(x) / I_{\nu-1}(x)$ for $\nu \ge 0.5$ and $x > 0$. We make use of the Perron continued fraction

$$
R_\nu(x) = \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

where $\gamma \in \mathbb R$ is an arbitrary constant and

$$
f(\nu,\gamma;x) = (2\nu -\gamma ) + \frac{-(2\nu+1)x}{2(\nu+x)+1+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+3)x}{2(\nu+x)+2+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+5)x}{2(\nu+x)+3+{}} \cdots
$$

The desired result is

$$
1-R_\nu(x) =\frac{\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

It is shown that the sequence of convergents, $(f_n)_{n=0}^\infty$, monotonically decreases toward $f$, and that

$$
\nu-0.5 <  \gamma+ f < \gamma+ f_n < 2\nu
$$

for all $n \ge 1$. The continued fraction $f$ is evaluated by $f_n$ for some $n \ge 1$ such that $|f_n-f_{n-1}| \le \epsilon |f_n|$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a given tolerance. The desired result is then evaluated by

$$
1-R_{\nu,n}(x) := \frac{\gamma+f_n}{x+\gamma+f_n}
$$

**Truncation error**.  When $1-R_\nu(x)$ is evaluated by $1-R_{\nu,n}(x)$, the relative truncation error is

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right|= \frac{x(f_n-f)}{(x+\gamma+f_n)(\gamma+f)}
$$

When the termination condition is satisfied, it is shown that

$$
\begin{align*}
f_n-f \le \epsilon | f_n| \frac{x}{2\nu-0.5}
\end{align*}
$$

(Note that the above bound is very coarse for large $x$.) Together with the fact that

$$
\frac{x}{x+\gamma+f_n} < \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f}=R
$$

and that

$$
\frac{1}{\gamma+f}=\frac{R}{x(1-R)},
$$

the relative truncation error may be bounded by

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right| < \frac{R^2}{1-R}\frac{\epsilon |f_n|}{2\nu-0.5}
$$

This bound can grow arbitrarily large as $R \rightarrow 1$, unless $f_n$ converges to $0$ “fast enough”. Thus, unlike `_iv_ratio`, the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` is not guaranteed even if infinite precision arithmetic were used. We proceed to test the accuracy numerically.

**Accuracy**. We test the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` numerically for each choice of $\gamma \in \\{0, \nu-0.5, 1.5\nu-0.15, 2\nu\\}$ and for various choices of $\epsilon$. For each $\gamma$ and $\epsilon$, a few values of $\nu$ are tested; for each $\nu$, 100,000 values of $x$ are chosen such that $R_\nu(x)$ is "approximately" evenly spaced over $(0,1)$. The computed result is then compared against reference values produced by `mpmath`.

The results show that the choice $\gamma=0$ consistently produces the smallest relative error. The accuracy improves with smaller $\epsilon$ but "flattens" after $2^{-56}$  Therefore, we choose $\gamma=0$ and $\epsilon=2^{-56}$ in this PR.

**Tail accuracy**. For really large $x$, it is too slow to compute the reference answer using `mpmath`. Instead, we use the asymptotic expansion

$$
R_\nu(x) = 1-\frac{\nu-0.5}{x}+\frac{(\nu-0.5)(\nu-1.5)}{2x^2} + O(x^{-3})
$$

for $\nu > 0.5$, and $R_{0.5}(x) \equiv \tanh(x)$. We test a few large $x$ for each choice of $\nu$. The result is summarized below.

**Asymptotic expansion**

From the asymptotic expansion of modified Bessel functions (NIST, 10.40.1, 10.17.1)

$$
I_\nu(z) =\frac{e^z}{\sqrt{2\pi z}} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\left(\frac12 -\nu\right)_k \left(\frac12+\nu\right)_k }{ 2^k k!} z^{-k}
%(-1)^k a_k(\nu) z^{-k}
$$

where

$$
(a)\_k := \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (a+i)
$$

$$
\frac{I_{\mu+1/2}(x)}{I_{\mu-1/2}(x)} = 1-\frac{\mu}{x} +\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^2}+\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^3}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^4\}\right)
$$

$$
1-\frac{I_{\mu+1/2}(x)}{I_{\mu-1/2}(x)} = \frac{\mu}{x} -\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^2}-\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^3}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^4\}\right)
$$

Reference issue
Toward gh-20253.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Adds a private function `_iv_ratio_c` to compute `1-iv(v,x)/iv(v-1,x)` for `v >= 1` and `x >= 0`. One of `v` or `x` may be `inf` but not both.

This is complementary to `_iv_ratio` (gh-20457) but offers better accuracy for large `x`, where `_iv_ratio(v,x)` is close to 1.

The purpose of this function is to be used to compute the inverse of `_iv_ratio` using a univariate root finder accurately when the function value is close to 1. Preliminary results show that this helps to reduce the relative error (of the inverse) from a few hundred machine epsilon to a few machine epsilon.

#### Algorithm
Following the lines of gh-20457, let $R_\nu(x) := I_\nu(x) / I_{\nu-1}(x)$ for $\nu \ge 0.5$ and $x > 0$. We make use of the Perron continued fraction

$$
R_\nu(x) = \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

where $\gamma \in \mathbb R$ is an arbitrary constant and

$$
f(\nu,\gamma;x) = (2\nu -\gamma ) + \frac{-(2\nu+1)x}{2(\nu+x)+1+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+3)x}{2(\nu+x)+2+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+5)x}{2(\nu+x)+3+{}} \cdots
$$

The desired result is

$$
1-R_\nu(x) =\frac{\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

It is shown that the sequence of convergents, $(f_n)_{n=0}^\infty$, monotonically decreases toward $f$, and that

$$
\nu-0.5 <  \gamma+ f < \gamma+ f_n < 2\nu
$$

for all $n \ge 1$. The continued fraction $f$ is evaluated by $f_n$ for some $n \ge 1$ such that $|f_n-f_{n-1}| \le \epsilon |f_n|$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a given tolerance. The desired result is then evaluated by

$$
1-R_{\nu,n}(x) := \frac{\gamma+f_n}{x+\gamma+f_n}
$$

**Truncation error**.  When $1-R_\nu(x)$ is evaluated by $1-R_{\nu,n}(x)$, the relative truncation error is

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right|= \frac{x(f_n-f)}{(x+\gamma+f_n)(\gamma+f)}
$$

When the termination condition is satisfied, it is shown that

$$
\begin{align*}
f_n-f \le \epsilon | f_n| \frac{x}{2\nu-0.5}
\end{align*}
$$

(Note that the above bound is very coarse for large $x$.) Together with the fact that

$$
\frac{x}{x+\gamma+f_n} < \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f}=R
$$

and that

$$
\frac{1}{\gamma+f}=\frac{R}{x(1-R)},
$$

the relative truncation error may be bounded by

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right| < \frac{R^2}{1-R}\frac{\epsilon |f_n|}{2\nu-0.5}
$$

This bound can grow arbitrarily large as $R \rightarrow 1$, unless $f_n$ converges to $0$ “fast enough”. Thus, unlike `_iv_ratio`, the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` is not guaranteed even if infinite precision arithmetic were used. We proceed to test the accuracy numerically.

**Accuracy**. We test the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` numerically for each choice of $\gamma \in \\{0, \nu-0.5, 1.5\nu-0.15, 2\nu\\}$ and for various choices of $\epsilon$. For each $\gamma$ and $\epsilon$, a few values of $\nu$ are tested; for each $\nu$, 100,000 values of $x$ are chosen such that $R_\nu(x)$ is "approximately" evenly spaced over $(0,1)$. The computed result is then compared against reference values produced by `mpmath`.

The results show that the choice $\gamma=0$ consistently produces the smallest relative error. The accuracy improves with smaller $\epsilon$ but "flattens" after $2^{-56}$  Therefore, we choose $\gamma=0$ and $\epsilon=2^{-56}$ in this PR.

$$
R_\nu(x) = 1-\frac{\nu-0.5}{x}+\frac{(\nu-0.5)(\nu-1.5)}{2x^2} + O(x^{-3})
$$

**Asymptotic expansion**

From the asymptotic expansion of modified Bessel functions (NIST, 10.40.1, 10.17.1)

$$
I_\nu(z) =\frac{e^z}{\sqrt{2\pi z}} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\left(\frac12 -\nu\right)_k \left(\frac12+\nu\right)_k }{ 2^k k!} z^{-k}
%(-1)^k a_k(\nu) z^{-k}
$$

where

$$
(a)\_k := \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (a+i)
$$

is the rising factorial, we can find (using the rules of multiplication and division of asymptotic expansion) that

$$
\frac{I_{\mu+1/2}(x)}{I_{\mu-1/2}(x)} = 1-\frac{\mu}{x} +\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^2}+\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^3}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^4\}\right)
$$

It follows that

$$
1-\frac{I_{\mu+1/2}(x)}{I_{\mu-1/2}(x)} = \frac{\mu}{x} -\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^2}-\frac{\mu(\mu-1)}{2x^3}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^4\}\right)
$$

Two special values that make the series finite are $\mu=0$ ($\nu=0.5$), for which

$$
\frac{I_{0.5}(x)}{I_{-0.5}(x)} = \tanh x, \\, 
1-\frac{I_{0.5}(x)}{I_{-0.5}(x)}= \frac{2e^{-2x}}{1+e^{-2x}},
$$

and $\mu=1$ ($\nu=1.5$), for which

$$

Reference issue
Toward gh-20253.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Adds a private function `_iv_ratio_c` to compute `1-iv(v,x)/iv(v-1,x)` for `v >= 1` and `x >= 0`. One of `v` or `x` may be `inf` but not both.

This is complementary to `_iv_ratio` (gh-20457) but offers better accuracy for large `x`, where `_iv_ratio(v,x)` is close to 1.

The purpose of this function is to be used to compute the inverse of `_iv_ratio` using a univariate root finder accurately when the function value is close to 1. Preliminary results show that this helps to reduce the relative error (of the inverse) from a few hundred machine epsilon to a few machine epsilon.

#### Algorithm
Following the lines of gh-20457, let $R_\nu(x) := I_\nu(x) / I_{\nu-1}(x)$ for $\nu \ge 0.5$ and $x > 0$. We make use of the Perron continued fraction

$$
R_\nu(x) = \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

where $\gamma \in \mathbb R$ is an arbitrary constant and

$$
f(\nu,\gamma;x) = (2\nu -\gamma ) + \frac{-(2\nu+1)x}{2(\nu+x)+1+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+3)x}{2(\nu+x)+2+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+5)x}{2(\nu+x)+3+{}} \cdots
$$

The desired result is

$$
1-R_\nu(x) =\frac{\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

It is shown that the sequence of convergents, $(f_n)_{n=0}^\infty$, monotonically decreases toward $f$, and that

$$
\nu-0.5 <  \gamma+ f < \gamma+ f_n < 2\nu
$$

for all $n \ge 1$. The continued fraction $f$ is evaluated by $f_n$ for some $n \ge 1$ such that $|f_n-f_{n-1}| \le \epsilon |f_n|$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a given tolerance. The desired result is then evaluated by

$$
1-R_{\nu,n}(x) := \frac{\gamma+f_n}{x+\gamma+f_n}
$$

**Truncation error**.  When $1-R_\nu(x)$ is evaluated by $1-R_{\nu,n}(x)$, the relative truncation error is

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right|= \frac{x(f_n-f)}{(x+\gamma+f_n)(\gamma+f)}
$$

When the termination condition is satisfied, it is shown that

$$
\begin{align*}
f_n-f \le \epsilon | f_n| \frac{x}{2\nu-0.5}
\end{align*}
$$

(Note that the above bound is very coarse for large $x$.) Together with the fact that

$$
\frac{x}{x+\gamma+f_n} < \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f}=R
$$

and that

$$
\frac{1}{\gamma+f}=\frac{R}{x(1-R)},
$$

the relative truncation error may be bounded by

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right| < \frac{R^2}{1-R}\frac{\epsilon |f_n|}{2\nu-0.5}
$$

This bound can grow arbitrarily large as $R \rightarrow 1$, unless $f_n$ converges to $0$ “fast enough”. Thus, unlike `_iv_ratio`, the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` is not guaranteed even if infinite precision arithmetic were used. We proceed to test the accuracy numerically.

**Accuracy**. We test the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` numerically for each choice of $\gamma \in \\{0, \nu-0.5, 1.5\nu-0.15, 2\nu\\}$ and for various choices of $\epsilon$. For each $\gamma$ and $\epsilon$, a few values of $\nu$ are tested; for each $\nu$, 100,000 values of $x$ are chosen such that $R_\nu(x)$ is "approximately" evenly spaced over $(0,1)$. The computed result is then compared against reference values produced by `mpmath`.

The results show that the choice $\gamma=0$ consistently produces the smallest relative error. The accuracy improves with smaller $\epsilon$ but "flattens" after $2^{-56}$  Therefore, we choose $\gamma=0$ and $\epsilon=2^{-56}$ in this PR.

%(-1)^k a_k(\nu) z^{-k}
$$

$$
(a)\_k := \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (a+i)

Reference issue
Toward gh-20253.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Adds a private function `_iv_ratio_c` to compute `1-iv(v,x)/iv(v-1,x)` for `v >= 1` and `x >= 0`. One of `v` or `x` may be `inf` but not both.

This is complementary to `_iv_ratio` (gh-20457) but offers better accuracy for large `x`, where `_iv_ratio(v,x)` is close to 1.

The purpose of this function is to be used to compute the inverse of `_iv_ratio` using a univariate root finder accurately when the function value is close to 1. Preliminary results show that this helps to reduce the relative error (of the inverse) from a few hundred machine epsilon to a few machine epsilon.

#### Algorithm
Following the lines of gh-20457, let $R_\nu(x) := I_\nu(x) / I_{\nu-1}(x)$ for $\nu \ge 0.5$ and $x > 0$. We make use of the Perron continued fraction

$$
R_\nu(x) = \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

where $\gamma \in \mathbb R$ is an arbitrary constant and

$$
f(\nu,\gamma;x) = (2\nu -\gamma ) + \frac{-(2\nu+1)x}{2(\nu+x)+1+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+3)x}{2(\nu+x)+2+{}} \frac{-(2\nu+5)x}{2(\nu+x)+3+{}} \cdots
$$

The desired result is

$$
1-R_\nu(x) =\frac{\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}{x+\gamma+f(\nu,\gamma;x)}
$$

It is shown that the sequence of convergents, $(f_n)_{n=0}^\infty$, monotonically decreases toward $f$, and that

$$
\nu-0.5 <  \gamma+ f < \gamma+ f_n < 2\nu
$$

for all $n \ge 1$. The continued fraction $f$ is evaluated by $f_n$ for some $n \ge 1$ such that $|f_n-f_{n-1}| \le \epsilon |f_n|$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a given tolerance. The desired result is then evaluated by

$$
1-R_{\nu,n}(x) := \frac{\gamma+f_n}{x+\gamma+f_n}
$$

**Truncation error**.  When $1-R_\nu(x)$ is evaluated by $1-R_{\nu,n}(x)$, the relative truncation error is

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right|= \frac{x(f_n-f)}{(x+\gamma+f_n)(\gamma+f)}
$$

When the termination condition is satisfied, it is shown that

$$
\begin{align*}
f_n-f \le \epsilon | f_n| \frac{x}{2\nu-0.5}
\end{align*}
$$

(Note that the above bound is very coarse for large $x$.) Together with the fact that

$$
\frac{x}{x+\gamma+f_n} < \frac{x}{x+\gamma+f}=R
$$

and that

$$
\frac{1}{\gamma+f}=\frac{R}{x(1-R)},
$$

the relative truncation error may be bounded by

$$
\left| \frac{1-R_{\nu,n}(x)}{1-R_\nu(x)} - 1\right| < \frac{R^2}{1-R}\frac{\epsilon |f_n|}{2\nu-0.5}
$$

This bound can grow arbitrarily large as $R \rightarrow 1$, unless $f_n$ converges to $0$ “fast enough”. Thus, unlike `_iv_ratio`, the accuracy of `_iv_ratio_c` is not guaranteed even if infinite precision arithmetic were used. We proceed to test the accuracy numerically.
