#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

##### Root finding

This PR implements scalar root-finding tools in xsf that we can use to bring functions from cdflib from the GPU. Rather than trying to translate the root finding tools from the current cdflib C translation, I rewrote them from scratch, following the Algol code in the paper [Two Efficient Algorithms with Guaranteed Convergence for Finding a Zero of a Function](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/355656.355659) by Bus and Dekker, for the implementation of the root finding algorithm used in cdflib, and writing an initial bracket finder based on the general idea from @mdhaber's [bracket_root](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/4d2c9e050663efd54396a3d8749792fad0b55dde/scipy/optimize/_elementwise.py#L462-L624), which itself uses well understood bracket finding techniques. I made some adjustments to accommodate searching over the entire range of double values. Both the root finding and bracket finding routines assume monotonicity.

The implementation of root finding tools in cdflib is hopelessly tangled, due its use of a reverse communication style which is a workaround for Fortran 77's lack of callbacks. I think the new implementation is much easier to follow, and because I'm able to understand, I was able to make some improvements. I had pointed out [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issuecomment-1902098317) that the cdflib implementation doesn't do a good job of letting you control convergence. The rate of convergence outspeeds the reported tolerance, so tolerance was set at 1e-8 originally, because setting the tolerance too low often caused additional jumps that lead to a worse solution. The new implementation uses a criterion which allows us to search to the limits of machine precision, which will be seen in the improvement in the quality of results.

##### gdtrib

I have implemented `gdtrib` from cdflib as a proof of concept. The work in this PR is only a small fraction of the work I've done relating to cdflib. I've translated much of it to C++, and benchmarked it's routines against those from cephes. Rather than using the incomplete gamma function routine from cdflib, I've opted to use `igam` and `igamc` from cephes, which are comparable in accuracy, and have the benefit of not allocating arrays internally; which means they can be used on the GPU. Cephes is also what is used in `gdtr`, so by using cephes, `gdtrib` becomes more of a proper inverse with respect to `b` of our `gdtr`. I think it would be good to follow a general principle that our inverse cdf functions invert the actual implementations we use for the `cdf`.

##### Unable to use std::function

One thing that is annoying, is that I couldn't have functions be passed to the root finding routines as `std::function`, and use capturing lambda's to construct functions within the inverse cdf functions to pass to the root finders. In order to make this work in CuPy using NVRTC, I needed to use function pointers of type `double (*func)(double, std::tuple<Args...>)`, where the tuple of args is for the distribution parameters that we'd like to be able to just capture in a lambda. The root finding routine itself takes a tuple of args, `std::tuple<Args...> args`, which we can use to specialize the function. I hope we can eventually get `std::function` and capturing lambda's to work in CuPy, but I think using function pointers like is a reasonable workaround for now.

##### Exceptional cases
I mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/20972#issuecomment-2267261963, that I'd like to try to fix the edge cases as I translate `cdflib`. In this regard, the changes I've made here are

* Expand the search space for the parameter `b` to all normalized positive doubles. Previously the search space was the interval `[1e-100, 1e100]`. The bracket finding algorithm I've written has no issues with the expanded search space.
* If the bracket finding algorithm determines that the actual root must be greater than the largest double, infinity is returned, and overflow is signaled with `set_error`. If it determines that the actual root must be smaller than the smallest normalized double, underflow is signaled and zero is returned.
* Limiting cases are handled explicitly. These are
    *  `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `x -> 0` when `p > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to infinity as `p -> 0` from the right when `x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `p -> 1.0` from the left when x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, 0, 0)` is indeterminate`
    I had noticed for instance that for the `p = 0` and `p = 1` cases, there will be a range of `b` values where `gdtr(a, b, x)` numerically evaluates to 0 or 1 respectively, and the old implementation would just return one of them, almost at random, depending upon the vagaries of how it's initial bracket finder is set up.

##### CuPy
I've verified that this works in CuPy and have added a test case to `scipy/special/tests/test_xsf_cuda.py`.

##### GPU Speedup
I used the following script to create a CuPy `ElementwiseKernel` for `gdtrib` and set up some large arrays to run it over, to compare timing with `gdtrib` on the CPU

```python
import cupy
import numpy as np
import scipy.special as sc



preamble = "#include <xsf/cdflib.h>"
routine = "out0 = xsf::gdtrib(in0, in1, in2)"
name = "gdtrib"
in_params = "float64 in0, float64 in1, float64 in2"
out_params = "float64 out0"


cupy_gdtrib = cupy.ElementwiseKernel(
    in_params, out_params, routine, name, preamble=preamble,
    options=(f"--include-path={sc._get_include()}", "-std=c++17"),
)

a = cupy.array(2.5)
p = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
x = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 10.0, 3000)
p, x = cupy.meshgrid(p, x)

A = 2.5

X = np.linspace(1e-10, 10, 3000)
```

##### Improvements in accuracy

I wrote a very rough script which I used to compare the new and old implementations along the following metrics

1. Accuracy of `gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`.
2. Accuracy of `mp_gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`. Where `mp_gdtr` is a correctly rounded version of `gdtr` which uses arbitrary precision internally and converts to float before returning.
3. Comparison of `gdtrib(a, p, x)` against an arbitrary precision reference.

Currently the old `gdtrib` remains in this branch under the name `gdtrib_old`, solely for benchmarking purposes. We'll need to take this out before this get merged.

<details>

First the script I used to generate the data

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mpmath import mp
from scipy.special import gdtrib, gdtrib_old, gdtr


def mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, guess):
    a, p, x = mp.mpf(a), mp.mpf(p), mp.mpf(x)
    def func(b):
        result = mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True) - p
        return result
    with mp.workdps(100):
        try:
            result = float(
                mp.findroot(
                    func,
                    guess,
                    verify=True,
                    tol=1e-30,
                )
            )
        except Exception:
            result = np.nan
    return result


def round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def mp_round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def func(a, p, x, b):
    q = 1 - p
    if p <= q:
        return gammainc(b, a*x) - p
    return q - gammaincc(b, a*x)


def neighbors(x, k):
    output = []
    horizon = np.inf
    if k < 0:
        horizon = -horizon
        k = -k
    for i in range(k):
        x = np.nextafter(x, horizon)
        output.append(x)
    return np.asarray(output)


rng = np.random.default_rng(1729)

P = np.hstack(
    (
        rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10),
        neighbors(1.0, -3), # very close to 1.0,
    )
)
P = np.sort(P)
A = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12)
X = np.hstack(
    (rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12))
)

# gdtrib
p_array, a_array, x_array = np.meshgrid(P, A, X)
p_array, a_array, x_array = p_array.ravel(), a_array.ravel(), x_array.ravel()

results1 = []
results2 = []
expected = []
p_rt, p_rt_old, p_rt_mp, p_rt_mp_old = [], [], [], []
for p, a, x in zip(p_array, a_array, x_array):
    val1 = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    val2 = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    expected.append(mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, val2))
    results1.append(val1)
    results2.append(val2)
    p_rt.append(round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_old.append(round_trip_old(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp.append(mp_round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp_old.append(mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x))

results1 = np.asarray(results1)
results2 = np.asarray(results2)
expected = np.asarray(expected)
p_rt = np.asarray(p_rt)
p_rt_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)
p_rt_mp = np.asarray(p_rt_mp)
p_rt_mp_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "p": p_array,
        "a": a_array,
        "x": x_array,
        "results1": results1,
        "results2": results2,
        "expected": expected,
        "p_rt": p_rt,
        "p_rt_old": p_rt_old,
        "p_rt_mp": p_rt_mp,
        "p_rt_mp_old": p_rt_mp_old,
    }
)
```

##### Next steps
Although only one function from cdflib is made available on the GPU here, most of the work towards making this possible is in this PR, and after this gets in, it will be tedious but straightforward to follow through and make the rest of cdflib work on the GPU. 

Also, unrelated to this PR, I've found that we can significantly improve our implementation of the `gamma` function by combining the `cephes` and `cdflib` implementations, as suggested by @ilayn here https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issue-2069115062. I will eventually get around to this in a followup.

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

##### Root finding

This PR implements scalar root-finding tools in xsf that we can use to bring functions from cdflib from the GPU. Rather than trying to translate the root finding tools from the current cdflib C translation, I rewrote them from scratch, following the Algol code in the paper [Two Efficient Algorithms with Guaranteed Convergence for Finding a Zero of a Function](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/355656.355659) by Bus and Dekker, for the implementation of the root finding algorithm used in cdflib, and writing an initial bracket finder based on the general idea from @mdhaber's [bracket_root](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/4d2c9e050663efd54396a3d8749792fad0b55dde/scipy/optimize/_elementwise.py#L462-L624), which itself uses well understood bracket finding techniques. I made some adjustments to accommodate searching over the entire range of double values. Both the root finding and bracket finding routines assume monotonicity.

The implementation of root finding tools in cdflib is hopelessly tangled, due its use of a reverse communication style which is a workaround for Fortran 77's lack of callbacks. I think the new implementation is much easier to follow, and because I'm able to understand, I was able to make some improvements. I had pointed out [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issuecomment-1902098317) that the cdflib implementation doesn't do a good job of letting you control convergence. The rate of convergence outspeeds the reported tolerance, so tolerance was set at 1e-8 originally, because setting the tolerance too low often caused additional jumps that lead to a worse solution. The new implementation uses a criterion which allows us to search to the limits of machine precision, which will be seen in the improvement in the quality of results.

##### gdtrib

I have implemented `gdtrib` from cdflib as a proof of concept. The work in this PR is only a small fraction of the work I've done relating to cdflib. I've translated much of it to C++, and benchmarked it's routines against those from cephes. Rather than using the incomplete gamma function routine from cdflib, I've opted to use `igam` and `igamc` from cephes, which are comparable in accuracy, and have the benefit of not allocating arrays internally; which means they can be used on the GPU. Cephes is also what is used in `gdtr`, so by using cephes, `gdtrib` becomes more of a proper inverse with respect to `b` of our `gdtr`. I think it would be good to follow a general principle that our inverse cdf functions invert the actual implementations we use for the `cdf`.

##### Unable to use std::function

One thing that is annoying, is that I couldn't have functions be passed to the root finding routines as `std::function`, and use capturing lambda's to construct functions within the inverse cdf functions to pass to the root finders. In order to make this work in CuPy using NVRTC, I needed to use function pointers of type `double (*func)(double, std::tuple<Args...>)`, where the tuple of args is for the distribution parameters that we'd like to be able to just capture in a lambda. The root finding routine itself takes a tuple of args, `std::tuple<Args...> args`, which we can use to specialize the function. I hope we can eventually get `std::function` and capturing lambda's to work in CuPy, but I think using function pointers like is a reasonable workaround for now.

##### Exceptional cases
I mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/20972#issuecomment-2267261963, that I'd like to try to fix the edge cases as I translate `cdflib`. In this regard, the changes I've made here are

* Expand the search space for the parameter `b` to all normalized positive doubles. Previously the search space was the interval `[1e-100, 1e100]`. The bracket finding algorithm I've written has no issues with the expanded search space.
* If the bracket finding algorithm determines that the actual root must be greater than the largest double, infinity is returned, and overflow is signaled with `set_error`. If it determines that the actual root must be smaller than the smallest normalized double, underflow is signaled and zero is returned.
* Limiting cases are handled explicitly. These are
    *  `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `x -> 0` when `p > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to infinity as `p -> 0` from the right when `x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `p -> 1.0` from the left when x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, 0, 0)` is indeterminate`
    I had noticed for instance that for the `p = 0` and `p = 1` cases, there will be a range of `b` values where `gdtr(a, b, x)` numerically evaluates to 0 or 1 respectively, and the old implementation would just return one of them, almost at random, depending upon the vagaries of how it's initial bracket finder is set up.

##### CuPy
I've verified that this works in CuPy and have added a test case to `scipy/special/tests/test_xsf_cuda.py`.

##### GPU Speedup
I used the following script to create a CuPy `ElementwiseKernel` for `gdtrib` and set up some large arrays to run it over, to compare timing with `gdtrib` on the CPU

```python
import cupy
import numpy as np
import scipy.special as sc



preamble = "#include <xsf/cdflib.h>"
routine = "out0 = xsf::gdtrib(in0, in1, in2)"
name = "gdtrib"
in_params = "float64 in0, float64 in1, float64 in2"
out_params = "float64 out0"


cupy_gdtrib = cupy.ElementwiseKernel(
    in_params, out_params, routine, name, preamble=preamble,
    options=(f"--include-path={sc._get_include()}", "-std=c++17"),
)

a = cupy.array(2.5)
p = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
x = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 10.0, 3000)
p, x = cupy.meshgrid(p, x)

A = 2.5
P = np.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
X = np.linspace(1e-10, 10, 3000)
P, X = np.meshgrid(P, X)

# Calling the function will invoke the JIT to compile the ElementwiseKernel. We don't compilation to be
# included in the timing
cupy_gdtrib(a, p[0], x[0])
```

and observed a roughly 5x speedup in Ipython using my NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU.

```

Wall time: 31.2 s
```
```

```

##### Improvements in accuracy

I wrote a very rough script which I used to compare the new and old implementations along the following metrics

1. Accuracy of `gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`.
2. Accuracy of `mp_gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`. Where `mp_gdtr` is a correctly rounded version of `gdtr` which uses arbitrary precision internally and converts to float before returning.
3. Comparison of `gdtrib(a, p, x)` against an arbitrary precision reference.

Currently the old `gdtrib` remains in this branch under the name `gdtrib_old`, solely for benchmarking purposes. We'll need to take this out before this get merged.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mpmath import mp
from scipy.special import gdtrib, gdtrib_old, gdtr


def mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, guess):
    a, p, x = mp.mpf(a), mp.mpf(p), mp.mpf(x)
    def func(b):
        result = mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True) - p
        return result
    with mp.workdps(100):
        try:
            result = float(
                mp.findroot(
                    func,
                    guess,
                    verify=True,
                    tol=1e-30,
                )
            )
        except Exception:
            result = np.nan
    return result


def round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def mp_round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def func(a, p, x, b):
    q = 1 - p
    if p <= q:
        return gammainc(b, a*x) - p
    return q - gammaincc(b, a*x)


def neighbors(x, k):
    output = []
    horizon = np.inf
    if k < 0:
        horizon = -horizon
        k = -k
    for i in range(k):
        x = np.nextafter(x, horizon)
        output.append(x)
    return np.asarray(output)


rng = np.random.default_rng(1729)

P = np.hstack(
    (
        rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10),
        neighbors(1.0, -3), # very close to 1.0,
    )
)
P = np.sort(P)
A = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12)
X = np.hstack(
    (rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12))
)

# gdtrib
p_array, a_array, x_array = np.meshgrid(P, A, X)
p_array, a_array, x_array = p_array.ravel(), a_array.ravel(), x_array.ravel()

results1 = []
results2 = []
expected = []
p_rt, p_rt_old, p_rt_mp, p_rt_mp_old = [], [], [], []
for p, a, x in zip(p_array, a_array, x_array):
    val1 = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    val2 = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    expected.append(mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, val2))
    results1.append(val1)
    results2.append(val2)
    p_rt.append(round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_old.append(round_trip_old(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp.append(mp_round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp_old.append(mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x))

results1 = np.asarray(results1)
results2 = np.asarray(results2)
expected = np.asarray(expected)
p_rt = np.asarray(p_rt)
p_rt_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)
p_rt_mp = np.asarray(p_rt_mp)
p_rt_mp_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "p": p_array,
        "a": a_array,
        "x": x_array,
        "results1": results1,
        "results2": results2,
        "expected": expected,
        "p_rt": p_rt,
        "p_rt_old": p_rt_old,
        "p_rt_mp": p_rt_mp,
        "p_rt_mp_old": p_rt_mp_old,
    }
)
```

##### Next steps
Although only one function from cdflib is made available on the GPU here, most of the work towards making this possible is in this PR, and after this gets in, it will be tedious but straightforward to follow through and make the rest of cdflib work on the GPU. 

Also, unrelated to this PR, I've found that we can significantly improve our implementation of the `gamma` function by combining the `cephes` and `cdflib` implementations, as suggested by @ilayn here https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issue-2069115062. I will eventually get around to this in a followup.

##### Root finding

This PR implements scalar root-finding tools in xsf that we can use to bring functions from cdflib from the GPU. Rather than trying to translate the root finding tools from the current cdflib C translation, I rewrote them from scratch, following the Algol code in the paper [Two Efficient Algorithms with Guaranteed Convergence for Finding a Zero of a Function](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/355656.355659) by Bus and Dekker, for the implementation of the root finding algorithm used in cdflib, and writing an initial bracket finder based on the general idea from @mdhaber's [bracket_root](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/4d2c9e050663efd54396a3d8749792fad0b55dde/scipy/optimize/_elementwise.py#L462-L624), which itself uses well understood bracket finding techniques. I made some adjustments to accommodate searching over the entire range of double values. Both the root finding and bracket finding routines assume monotonicity.

The implementation of root finding tools in cdflib is hopelessly tangled, due its use of a reverse communication style which is a workaround for Fortran 77's lack of callbacks. I think the new implementation is much easier to follow, and because I'm able to understand, I was able to make some improvements. I had pointed out [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issuecomment-1902098317) that the cdflib implementation doesn't do a good job of letting you control convergence. The rate of convergence outspeeds the reported tolerance, so tolerance was set at 1e-8 originally, because setting the tolerance too low often caused additional jumps that lead to a worse solution. The new implementation uses a criterion which allows us to search to the limits of machine precision, which will be seen in the improvement in the quality of results.

##### gdtrib

I have implemented `gdtrib` from cdflib as a proof of concept. The work in this PR is only a small fraction of the work I've done relating to cdflib. I've translated much of it to C++, and benchmarked it's routines against those from cephes. Rather than using the incomplete gamma function routine from cdflib, I've opted to use `igam` and `igamc` from cephes, which are comparable in accuracy, and have the benefit of not allocating arrays internally; which means they can be used on the GPU. Cephes is also what is used in `gdtr`, so by using cephes, `gdtrib` becomes more of a proper inverse with respect to `b` of our `gdtr`. I think it would be good to follow a general principle that our inverse cdf functions invert the actual implementations we use for the `cdf`.

##### Unable to use std::function

One thing that is annoying, is that I couldn't have functions be passed to the root finding routines as `std::function`, and use capturing lambda's to construct functions within the inverse cdf functions to pass to the root finders. In order to make this work in CuPy using NVRTC, I needed to use function pointers of type `double (*func)(double, std::tuple<Args...>)`, where the tuple of args is for the distribution parameters that we'd like to be able to just capture in a lambda. The root finding routine itself takes a tuple of args, `std::tuple<Args...> args`, which we can use to specialize the function. I hope we can eventually get `std::function` and capturing lambda's to work in CuPy, but I think using function pointers like is a reasonable workaround for now.

##### Exceptional cases
I mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/20972#issuecomment-2267261963, that I'd like to try to fix the edge cases as I translate `cdflib`. In this regard, the changes I've made here are

* Expand the search space for the parameter `b` to all normalized positive doubles. Previously the search space was the interval `[1e-100, 1e100]`. The bracket finding algorithm I've written has no issues with the expanded search space.
* If the bracket finding algorithm determines that the actual root must be greater than the largest double, infinity is returned, and overflow is signaled with `set_error`. If it determines that the actual root must be smaller than the smallest normalized double, underflow is signaled and zero is returned.
* Limiting cases are handled explicitly. These are
    *  `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `x -> 0` when `p > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to infinity as `p -> 0` from the right when `x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `p -> 1.0` from the left when x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, 0, 0)` is indeterminate`
    I had noticed for instance that for the `p = 0` and `p = 1` cases, there will be a range of `b` values where `gdtr(a, b, x)` numerically evaluates to 0 or 1 respectively, and the old implementation would just return one of them, almost at random, depending upon the vagaries of how it's initial bracket finder is set up.

##### CuPy
I've verified that this works in CuPy and have added a test case to `scipy/special/tests/test_xsf_cuda.py`.

##### GPU Speedup
I used the following script to create a CuPy `ElementwiseKernel` for `gdtrib` and set up some large arrays to run it over, to compare timing with `gdtrib` on the CPU

```python
import cupy
import numpy as np
import scipy.special as sc



preamble = "#include <xsf/cdflib.h>"
routine = "out0 = xsf::gdtrib(in0, in1, in2)"
name = "gdtrib"
in_params = "float64 in0, float64 in1, float64 in2"
out_params = "float64 out0"


cupy_gdtrib = cupy.ElementwiseKernel(
    in_params, out_params, routine, name, preamble=preamble,
    options=(f"--include-path={sc._get_include()}", "-std=c++17"),
)

a = cupy.array(2.5)
p = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
x = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 10.0, 3000)
p, x = cupy.meshgrid(p, x)

A = 2.5
P = np.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
X = np.linspace(1e-10, 10, 3000)
P, X = np.meshgrid(P, X)

# Calling the function will invoke the JIT to compile the ElementwiseKernel. We don't compilation to be
# included in the timing
cupy_gdtrib(a, p[0], x[0])
```

##### Improvements in accuracy

I wrote a very rough script which I used to compare the new and old implementations along the following metrics

1. Accuracy of `gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`.
2. Accuracy of `mp_gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`. Where `mp_gdtr` is a correctly rounded version of `gdtr` which uses arbitrary precision internally and converts to float before returning.
3. Comparison of `gdtrib(a, p, x)` against an arbitrary precision reference.

Currently the old `gdtrib` remains in this branch under the name `gdtrib_old`, solely for benchmarking purposes. We'll need to take this out before this get merged.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mpmath import mp
from scipy.special import gdtrib, gdtrib_old, gdtr


def mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, guess):
    a, p, x = mp.mpf(a), mp.mpf(p), mp.mpf(x)
    def func(b):
        result = mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True) - p
        return result
    with mp.workdps(100):
        try:
            result = float(
                mp.findroot(
                    func,
                    guess,
                    verify=True,
                    tol=1e-30,
                )
            )
        except Exception:
            result = np.nan
    return result


def round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def mp_round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def func(a, p, x, b):
    q = 1 - p
    if p <= q:
        return gammainc(b, a*x) - p
    return q - gammaincc(b, a*x)


def neighbors(x, k):
    output = []
    horizon = np.inf
    if k < 0:
        horizon = -horizon
        k = -k
    for i in range(k):
        x = np.nextafter(x, horizon)
        output.append(x)
    return np.asarray(output)


rng = np.random.default_rng(1729)

P = np.hstack(
    (
        rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10),
        neighbors(1.0, -3), # very close to 1.0,
    )
)
P = np.sort(P)
A = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12)
X = np.hstack(
    (rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12))
)

# gdtrib
p_array, a_array, x_array = np.meshgrid(P, A, X)
p_array, a_array, x_array = p_array.ravel(), a_array.ravel(), x_array.ravel()

results1 = []
results2 = []
expected = []
p_rt, p_rt_old, p_rt_mp, p_rt_mp_old = [], [], [], []
for p, a, x in zip(p_array, a_array, x_array):
    val1 = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    val2 = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    expected.append(mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, val2))
    results1.append(val1)
    results2.append(val2)
    p_rt.append(round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_old.append(round_trip_old(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp.append(mp_round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp_old.append(mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x))

results1 = np.asarray(results1)
results2 = np.asarray(results2)
expected = np.asarray(expected)
p_rt = np.asarray(p_rt)
p_rt_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)
p_rt_mp = np.asarray(p_rt_mp)
p_rt_mp_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "p": p_array,
        "a": a_array,

        "results1": results1,
        "results2": results2,
        "expected": expected,

        "p_rt_old": p_rt_old,
        "p_rt_mp": p_rt_mp,
        "p_rt_mp_old": p_rt_mp_old,
    }
)
```

Thanks for explaining. Indeed for use cases where the root is very far away from the initial bracket, the “plateau” handling is a viable optimization.

I tried to get a better understanding of the plateau handling behavior. Let $c$ denote `factor`. Let $(a_0,b_0)$ be first the bracket where $f(a_0)=f(b_0)$, so plateau handling kicks in. Let $\Delta=b_0-a_0$. I find that the following brackets, $(a_k,b_k)$, $k=1,2,3,\cdots$ have $a_k=a_0$, $b_k =a_0+(1+c)^k\Delta$, until some $b_k$ where $f(b_k)\ne f(a_0)$. This is where the function “goes out” of the plateau. If $f(b_k)$ has the opposite sign of $f(a_0)$, then it looks like $(a_0,b_k)$ is returned, which is probably a large interval.

In comparison, if plateau does not kick in, then I find $a_k=b_{k-1}$, $b_k=a_0+[(c^{k+1}-1)/(c-1)]\Delta$.

So the bracket size increment rate difference between non-plateau and plateau is basically a factor of $c$ versus a factor of $(1+c)$. Therefore I think the code could be simplified by multiplying the step size by `(1+factor)` if `y_frontier == y_interior` or by `factor` otherwise. There would be no need to “fix” `interior` in the plateau case, and the `plateau` variable could be dropped. #### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

##### Root finding

This PR implements scalar root-finding tools in xsf that we can use to bring functions from cdflib from the GPU. Rather than trying to translate the root finding tools from the current cdflib C translation, I rewrote them from scratch, following the Algol code in the paper [Two Efficient Algorithms with Guaranteed Convergence for Finding a Zero of a Function](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/355656.355659) by Bus and Dekker, for the implementation of the root finding algorithm used in cdflib, and writing an initial bracket finder based on the general idea from @mdhaber's [bracket_root](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/4d2c9e050663efd54396a3d8749792fad0b55dde/scipy/optimize/_elementwise.py#L462-L624), which itself uses well understood bracket finding techniques. I made some adjustments to accommodate searching over the entire range of double values. Both the root finding and bracket finding routines assume monotonicity.

The implementation of root finding tools in cdflib is hopelessly tangled, due its use of a reverse communication style which is a workaround for Fortran 77's lack of callbacks. I think the new implementation is much easier to follow, and because I'm able to understand, I was able to make some improvements. I had pointed out [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issuecomment-1902098317) that the cdflib implementation doesn't do a good job of letting you control convergence. The rate of convergence outspeeds the reported tolerance, so tolerance was set at 1e-8 originally, because setting the tolerance too low often caused additional jumps that lead to a worse solution. The new implementation uses a criterion which allows us to search to the limits of machine precision, which will be seen in the improvement in the quality of results.

##### gdtrib

I have implemented `gdtrib` from cdflib as a proof of concept. The work in this PR is only a small fraction of the work I've done relating to cdflib. I've translated much of it to C++, and benchmarked it's routines against those from cephes. Rather than using the incomplete gamma function routine from cdflib, I've opted to use `igam` and `igamc` from cephes, which are comparable in accuracy, and have the benefit of not allocating arrays internally; which means they can be used on the GPU. Cephes is also what is used in `gdtr`, so by using cephes, `gdtrib` becomes more of a proper inverse with respect to `b` of our `gdtr`. I think it would be good to follow a general principle that our inverse cdf functions invert the actual implementations we use for the `cdf`.

##### Unable to use std::function

One thing that is annoying, is that I couldn't have functions be passed to the root finding routines as `std::function`, and use capturing lambda's to construct functions within the inverse cdf functions to pass to the root finders. In order to make this work in CuPy using NVRTC, I needed to use function pointers of type `double (*func)(double, std::tuple<Args...>)`, where the tuple of args is for the distribution parameters that we'd like to be able to just capture in a lambda. The root finding routine itself takes a tuple of args, `std::tuple<Args...> args`, which we can use to specialize the function. I hope we can eventually get `std::function` and capturing lambda's to work in CuPy, but I think using function pointers like is a reasonable workaround for now.

##### Exceptional cases
I mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/20972#issuecomment-2267261963, that I'd like to try to fix the edge cases as I translate `cdflib`. In this regard, the changes I've made here are

* Expand the search space for the parameter `b` to all normalized positive doubles. Previously the search space was the interval `[1e-100, 1e100]`. The bracket finding algorithm I've written has no issues with the expanded search space.
* If the bracket finding algorithm determines that the actual root must be greater than the largest double, infinity is returned, and overflow is signaled with `set_error`. If it determines that the actual root must be smaller than the smallest normalized double, underflow is signaled and zero is returned.
* Limiting cases are handled explicitly. These are
    *  `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `x -> 0` when `p > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to infinity as `p -> 0` from the right when `x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `p -> 1.0` from the left when x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, 0, 0)` is indeterminate`
    I had noticed for instance that for the `p = 0` and `p = 1` cases, there will be a range of `b` values where `gdtr(a, b, x)` numerically evaluates to 0 or 1 respectively, and the old implementation would just return one of them, almost at random, depending upon the vagaries of how it's initial bracket finder is set up.

##### CuPy
I've verified that this works in CuPy and have added a test case to `scipy/special/tests/test_xsf_cuda.py`.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->
##### GPU Speedup
I used the following script to create a CuPy `ElementwiseKernel` for `gdtrib` and set up some large arrays to run it over, to compare timing with `gdtrib` on the CPU

```python
import cupy
import numpy as np
import scipy.special as sc



preamble = "#include <xsf/cdflib.h>"
routine = "out0 = xsf::gdtrib(in0, in1, in2)"
name = "gdtrib"
in_params = "float64 in0, float64 in1, float64 in2"
out_params = "float64 out0"


cupy_gdtrib = cupy.ElementwiseKernel(
    in_params, out_params, routine, name, preamble=preamble,
    options=(f"--include-path={sc._get_include()}", "-std=c++17"),
)

a = cupy.array(2.5)
p = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
x = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 10.0, 3000)
p, x = cupy.meshgrid(p, x)

A = 2.5
P = np.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
X = np.linspace(1e-10, 10, 3000)
P, X = np.meshgrid(P, X)

# Calling the function will invoke the JIT to compile the ElementwiseKernel. We don't compilation to be
# included in the timing
cupy_gdtrib(a, p[0], x[0])
```

and observed a roughly 5x speedup in Ipython using my NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU.

```
In [2] %time sc.gdtrib(A, P, X)
CPU times: user 31.2 s, sys: 0 ns, total: 31.2 s
Wall time: 31.2 s
```

```
In [3] %time cupy_gdtrib(a, p, x).get()
CPU times: user 6.29 s, sys: 11.7 ms, total: 6.3 s
Wall time: 6.3 s
```

##### Improvements in accuracy

I wrote a very rough script which I used to compare the new and old implementations along the following metrics

1. Accuracy of `gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`.
2. Accuracy of `mp_gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`. Where `mp_gdtr` is a correctly rounded version of `gdtr` which uses arbitrary precision internally and converts to float before returning.
3. Comparison of `gdtrib(a, p, x)` against an arbitrary precision reference.

Currently the old `gdtrib` remains in this branch under the name `gdtrib_old`, solely for benchmarking purposes. We'll need to take this out before this get merged.

First the script I used to generate the data

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mpmath import mp
from scipy.special import gdtrib, gdtrib_old, gdtr


def mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, guess):
    a, p, x = mp.mpf(a), mp.mpf(p), mp.mpf(x)
    def func(b):
        result = mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True) - p
        return result
    with mp.workdps(100):
        try:
            result = float(
                mp.findroot(
                    func,
                    guess,
                    verify=True,
                    tol=1e-30,
                )
            )
        except Exception:
            result = np.nan
    return result


def round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def mp_round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def func(a, p, x, b):
    q = 1 - p
    if p <= q:
        return gammainc(b, a*x) - p
    return q - gammaincc(b, a*x)


def neighbors(x, k):
    output = []
    horizon = np.inf
    if k < 0:
        horizon = -horizon
        k = -k
    for i in range(k):
        x = np.nextafter(x, horizon)
        output.append(x)
    return np.asarray(output)


rng = np.random.default_rng(1729)

P = np.hstack(
    (
        rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10),
        neighbors(1.0, -3), # very close to 1.0,
    )
)
P = np.sort(P)
A = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12)
X = np.hstack(
    (rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12))
)

# gdtrib
p_array, a_array, x_array = np.meshgrid(P, A, X)
p_array, a_array, x_array = p_array.ravel(), a_array.ravel(), x_array.ravel()

results1 = []
results2 = []
expected = []
p_rt, p_rt_old, p_rt_mp, p_rt_mp_old = [], [], [], []
for p, a, x in zip(p_array, a_array, x_array):
    val1 = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    val2 = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    expected.append(mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, val2))
    results1.append(val1)
    results2.append(val2)
    p_rt.append(round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_old.append(round_trip_old(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp.append(mp_round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp_old.append(mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x))

results1 = np.asarray(results1)
results2 = np.asarray(results2)
expected = np.asarray(expected)
p_rt = np.asarray(p_rt)
p_rt_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)
p_rt_mp = np.asarray(p_rt_mp)
p_rt_mp_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "p": p_array,
        "a": a_array,
        "x": x_array,
        "results1": results1,
        "results2": results2,
        "expected": expected,
        "p_rt": p_rt,
        "p_rt_old": p_rt_old,
        "p_rt_mp": p_rt_mp,
        "p_rt_mp_old": p_rt_mp_old,
    }
)
```

##### Next steps
Although only one function from cdflib is made available on the GPU here, most of the work towards making this possible is in this PR, and after this gets in, it will be tedious but straightforward to follow through and make the rest of cdflib work on the GPU. 

Also, unrelated to this PR, I've found that we can significantly improve our implementation of the `gamma` function by combining the `cephes` and `cdflib` implementations, as suggested by @ilayn here https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issue-2069115062. I will eventually get around to this in a followup.

cc @rlucas7 for review, @izaid in case you want to take a look at this, @fancidev for any suggestions you might have, @WarrenWeckesser since you've been active in `special` lately and might be interested in this.

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

##### Root finding

This PR implements scalar root-finding tools in xsf that we can use to bring functions from cdflib from the GPU. Rather than trying to translate the root finding tools from the current cdflib C translation, I rewrote them from scratch, following the Algol code in the paper [Two Efficient Algorithms with Guaranteed Convergence for Finding a Zero of a Function](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/355656.355659) by Bus and Dekker, for the implementation of the root finding algorithm used in cdflib, and writing an initial bracket finder based on the general idea from @mdhaber's [bracket_root](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/4d2c9e050663efd54396a3d8749792fad0b55dde/scipy/optimize/_elementwise.py#L462-L624), which itself uses well understood bracket finding techniques. I made some adjustments to accommodate searching over the entire range of double values. Both the root finding and bracket finding routines assume monotonicity.

The implementation of root finding tools in cdflib is hopelessly tangled, due its use of a reverse communication style which is a workaround for Fortran 77's lack of callbacks. I think the new implementation is much easier to follow, and because I'm able to understand, I was able to make some improvements. I had pointed out [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issuecomment-1902098317) that the cdflib implementation doesn't do a good job of letting you control convergence. The rate of convergence outspeeds the reported tolerance, so tolerance was set at 1e-8 originally, because setting the tolerance too low often caused additional jumps that lead to a worse solution. The new implementation uses a criterion which allows us to search to the limits of machine precision, which will be seen in the improvement in the quality of results.

##### gdtrib

I have implemented `gdtrib` from cdflib as a proof of concept. The work in this PR is only a small fraction of the work I've done relating to cdflib. I've translated much of it to C++, and benchmarked it's routines against those from cephes. Rather than using the incomplete gamma function routine from cdflib, I've opted to use `igam` and `igamc` from cephes, which are comparable in accuracy, and have the benefit of not allocating arrays internally; which means they can be used on the GPU. Cephes is also what is used in `gdtr`, so by using cephes, `gdtrib` becomes more of a proper inverse with respect to `b` of our `gdtr`. I think it would be good to follow a general principle that our inverse cdf functions invert the actual implementations we use for the `cdf`.

##### Unable to use std::function

One thing that is annoying, is that I couldn't have functions be passed to the root finding routines as `std::function`, and use capturing lambda's to construct functions within the inverse cdf functions to pass to the root finders. In order to make this work in CuPy using NVRTC, I needed to use function pointers of type `double (*func)(double, std::tuple<Args...>)`, where the tuple of args is for the distribution parameters that we'd like to be able to just capture in a lambda. The root finding routine itself takes a tuple of args, `std::tuple<Args...> args`, which we can use to specialize the function. I hope we can eventually get `std::function` and capturing lambda's to work in CuPy, but I think using function pointers like is a reasonable workaround for now.

##### Exceptional cases
I mentioned in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/20972#issuecomment-2267261963, that I'd like to try to fix the edge cases as I translate `cdflib`. In this regard, the changes I've made here are

* Expand the search space for the parameter `b` to all normalized positive doubles. Previously the search space was the interval `[1e-100, 1e100]`. The bracket finding algorithm I've written has no issues with the expanded search space.
* If the bracket finding algorithm determines that the actual root must be greater than the largest double, infinity is returned, and overflow is signaled with `set_error`. If it determines that the actual root must be smaller than the smallest normalized double, underflow is signaled and zero is returned.
* Limiting cases are handled explicitly. These are
    *  `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `x -> 0` when `p > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to infinity as `p -> 0` from the right when `x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, p, x)` tends to 0 as `p -> 1.0` from the left when x > 0`.
    * `gdtrib(a, 0, 0)` is indeterminate`
    I had noticed for instance that for the `p = 0` and `p = 1` cases, there will be a range of `b` values where `gdtr(a, b, x)` numerically evaluates to 0 or 1 respectively, and the old implementation would just return one of them, almost at random, depending upon the vagaries of how it's initial bracket finder is set up.

##### CuPy
I've verified that this works in CuPy and have added a test case to `scipy/special/tests/test_xsf_cuda.py`.

##### GPU Speedup
I used the following script to create a CuPy `ElementwiseKernel` for `gdtrib` and set up some large arrays to run it over, to compare timing with `gdtrib` on the CPU

```python
import cupy
import numpy as np
import scipy.special as sc



preamble = "#include <xsf/cdflib.h>"
routine = "out0 = xsf::gdtrib(in0, in1, in2)"
name = "gdtrib"
in_params = "float64 in0, float64 in1, float64 in2"
out_params = "float64 out0"


cupy_gdtrib = cupy.ElementwiseKernel(
    in_params, out_params, routine, name, preamble=preamble,
    options=(f"--include-path={sc._get_include()}", "-std=c++17"),
)

a = cupy.array(2.5)
p = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
x = cupy.linspace(1e-10, 10.0, 3000)
p, x = cupy.meshgrid(p, x)

A = 2.5
P = np.linspace(1e-10, 1, 3000)
X = np.linspace(1e-10, 10, 3000)
P, X = np.meshgrid(P, X)

# Calling the function will invoke the JIT to compile the ElementwiseKernel. We don't compilation to be
# included in the timing
cupy_gdtrib(a, p[0], x[0])
```

and observed a roughly 5x speedup in Ipython using my NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU.

```
In [2] %time sc.gdtrib(A, P, X)
CPU times: user 31.2 s, sys: 0 ns, total: 31.2 s
Wall time: 31.2 s
```

```

```

##### Improvements in accuracy

I wrote a very rough script which I used to compare the new and old implementations along the following metrics

1. Accuracy of `gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`.
2. Accuracy of `mp_gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)` in estimating `p`. Where `mp_gdtr` is a correctly rounded version of `gdtr` which uses arbitrary precision internally and converts to float before returning.
3. Comparison of `gdtrib(a, p, x)` against an arbitrary precision reference.

Currently the old `gdtrib` remains in this branch under the name `gdtrib_old`, solely for benchmarking purposes. We'll need to take this out before this get merged.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mpmath import mp
from scipy.special import gdtrib, gdtrib_old, gdtr


def mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, guess):
    a, p, x = mp.mpf(a), mp.mpf(p), mp.mpf(x)
    def func(b):
        result = mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True) - p
        return result
    with mp.workdps(100):
        try:
            result = float(
                mp.findroot(
                    func,
                    guess,
                    verify=True,
                    tol=1e-30,
                )
            )
        except Exception:
            result = np.nan
    return result


def round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    return gdtr(a, b, x)

def mp_round_trip(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x):
    b = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    with mp.workdps(30):
        try:
            result = float(mp.gammainc(b, 0, a*x, regularized=True))
        except Exception:
            return np.nan
    return result


def func(a, p, x, b):
    q = 1 - p
    if p <= q:
        return gammainc(b, a*x) - p
    return q - gammaincc(b, a*x)


def neighbors(x, k):
    output = []
    horizon = np.inf
    if k < 0:
        horizon = -horizon
        k = -k
    for i in range(k):
        x = np.nextafter(x, horizon)
        output.append(x)
    return np.asarray(output)


rng = np.random.default_rng(1729)

P = np.hstack(
    (
        rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10),
        neighbors(1.0, -3), # very close to 1.0,
    )
)
P = np.sort(P)
A = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12)
X = np.hstack(
    (rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, size=16) * 2.0**np.arange(-4, 12))
)

# gdtrib
p_array, a_array, x_array = np.meshgrid(P, A, X)
p_array, a_array, x_array = p_array.ravel(), a_array.ravel(), x_array.ravel()

results1 = []
results2 = []
expected = []
p_rt, p_rt_old, p_rt_mp, p_rt_mp_old = [], [], [], []
for p, a, x in zip(p_array, a_array, x_array):
    val1 = gdtrib(a, p, x)
    val2 = gdtrib_old(a, p, x)
    expected.append(mp_gdtrib(a, p, x, val2))
    results1.append(val1)
    results2.append(val2)
    p_rt.append(round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_old.append(round_trip_old(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp.append(mp_round_trip(p, a, x))
    p_rt_mp_old.append(mp_round_trip_old(p, a, x))

results1 = np.asarray(results1)
results2 = np.asarray(results2)
expected = np.asarray(expected)
p_rt = np.asarray(p_rt)
p_rt_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)
p_rt_mp = np.asarray(p_rt_mp)
p_rt_mp_old = np.asarray(p_rt_old)

        "p_rt_mp": p_rt_mp,
```

##### Next steps
Although only one function from cdflib is made available on the GPU here, most of the work towards making this possible is in this PR, and after this gets in, it will be tedious but straightforward to follow through and make the rest of cdflib work on the GPU. 

Also, unrelated to this PR, I've found that we can significantly improve our implementation of the `gamma` function by combining the `cephes` and `cdflib` implementations, as suggested by @ilayn here https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19824#issue-2069115062. I will eventually get around to this in a followup.

cc @rlucas7 for review, @izaid in case you want to take a look at this, @fancidev for any suggestions you might have, @WarrenWeckesser since you've been active in `special` lately and might be interested in this.

Reference issue
Toward gh-21404.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Adds a function `scipy.special.pow1p(x,y)` that computes `(1+x)**y` for real `x` and `y` for accurately than the direct formula.

It conforms to the IEEE-754 spec of the `pow` function except that (the `special` equivalent of) floating point exceptions may not be raised.

#### Additional information
Support for complex `x` and `y` may be added by a separate PR in the future.

#### Reference

[De71] Dekker, T. J. (1971) “A floating-point technique for extending the available precision.” _Numerische Mathematik_, 18:224–242.

[Mu16] Muller, J. M. (2016) Elementary Functions: Algorithms and Implementation. Birkhauser.

[Mu18] Muller, J. M. *et al* (2018) Handbook of Floating-Point Arithmetic. Birkhauser.

#### Notations and assumptions

We assume floating point numbers are representable as $`\pm d_0.d_1 d_2 \cdots d_{p-1} \times 2^e `$, where $d_i \in \\{0,1\\}$, $e_\min \le e \le e_\max$, $e_\min=1-e_\max$. The “weight” of $d_i$ is $2^{-i}$. A *normalized* number has $d_0=1$. A *subnormal* number has $d_0=0$ and $e=e_\min$. Let $\epsilon := 2^{-p+1}$ denote the *machine epsilon*. Let $\lambda:=2^{e_\min}$ denote the smallest normalized number. The smallest subnormal number is $\lambda \epsilon$.

<details>

For `binary64` type, $p=53$, $e_\min=-1022$, $e_\max=1023$, $\epsilon=2^{-52}\approx 2.22\times 10^{-16}$.

</details>

Let $\mathrm{RU}(\cdot)$ denote round toward $+\infty$, $\mathrm{RD}(\cdot)$ denote round toward $-\infty$, and $\mathrm{RN}(\cdot)$ denote round to nearest with ties resolved in any way. If $\mathrm{RN}(x)$ is normalized, then $|x-\mathrm{RN(x)}| \le 0.5\epsilon |x|$, and $|x-\mathrm{RN(x)}| \le 0.5\epsilon |\mathrm{RN}(x)|$.

Let $z \in \mathbb{R}$, $|z| < 1$. Then the following simple bounds hold:

(1) $\ln(1+z)=z(1+\delta)$ for some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\delta| \le (|z|/2)/(1-|z|)$.

(2) $\ln(1+z)=(z-z^2/2)(1+\delta)$ for some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\delta| \le (|z|^2/3)/(1-|z|/2)^2$.

(3) $e^{z}-1 = z(1+\delta)$ some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\delta| \le (|z|/2)/(1-|z|)$.

<details>

*Proof*. (1) and (2) follow from the Taylor series $\ln(1+z)=z-z^2 /2+  z^3/3 - z^4/4 + \cdots$ for $|z| < 1$. For (1), we have $|\ln(1+z)-z| = | -z^2/2 +  z^3/3 -  z^4/4 + \cdots |$ $\le  |z|^2/2 +  |z|^3/2 +  |z|^4/2 + \cdots$ $=  ( |z|^2/2) /(1-|z|)$. Dividing both sides by $|z|$ yields the desired result. For (2), we have $|\ln(1+z)-(z-z^2/2)| = |  z^3/3- z^4/4+\cdots |$ $\le  |z|^3/3 + |z|^4/3+\cdots$ $=( |z^3|/3)/(1-|z|)$. Dividing both sides by $|z-z^2/2|$ and relaxing  $1/(1-|z|)$ to $1/(1-|z|/2)$ yields the desired result.

#### Preliminary analysis

The computation of $x^y$ is briefly discussed in [Mu06] (Section 13.2). Even if the standard library function `pow(x,y)`  produces an accurate result (say to 1 ULP) for *exact*  $x$ and $y$, $(1+x)$ may not be exactly representable, in which case its rounding error would be magnified $y$ times by taking the power, since $(\mathrm{d}x^y /x^y )/(\mathrm{d}x/x)=y$. This leads to severe loss of precision e.g. for $|x | < \epsilon/2$ and large $y$.

For $x > -1$, an alternative is to evaluate $(1+x)^y$ by $e^{y\ln (1+x)}$. Again, unless $y\ln(1+x)$ is exactly representable, which is unlikely,  its rounding error gets magnified by  the exponentiation, since $(\mathrm{d} e^z / e^z)/({\mathrm{d} z / z} )= z$. Fortunately, we only have to worry about $z=y\ln(1+x)$ of magnitude not too large to cause overflow or underflow in the first place; this greatly restricts the range of interesting $z$ to $(e_\min-p) \ln 2 < z < (e_\max+1)\ln 2$. 

<details>

Overflow starts from $(2-\epsilon/2)\times 2^{e_\max}$; therefore the absence of overflow means $e^z < (2-\epsilon/2)\times 2^{e_\max} < 2^{e_\max+1}$, which implies $z < (e_\max+1) \ln 2 < 0.7(e_\max+1)$. A similar analysis shows $z > 0.7(e_\min-p)$ if $e^z$ does not underflow to zero.

For `binary64`, this means the relative error in the exponent is magnified by no more than 717 or -753 times. This magnification factor is much lower than that of the direct formula.

</details>

One way to compensate for the error magnification is to compute the exponent with higher precision. For example, if an extended precision type with $\log_2[(p-e_\min)\ln2]$ additional bits of significand is available, then we can accurately evaluate $(1+x)^y$ by `exp(y*log1p(x))` in the extended precision.

In the remaining, we describe an algorithm  to evaluate $(1+x)^y$ accurately when no extended precision data type is available.

After handling the special cases as prescribed by IEEE-754, we are left with finite (floating-point numbers) $x$ and $y$ that fall into two cases:

1. $x >-1$, $y \in \mathbb{R}$;
2. $x < -1$, $y \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Let’s first examine the case $x >-1$, $y \in \mathbb{R}$, which is probably more common. The key idea is to write 

$$
(1+x)^y = s^y (1+t/s)^y = s^y e^{y \ln(1+t/s)}
$$

for some $|t| \ll |s|$, and evaluate each power accurately. The algorithm is outlined below:

- Step 1: Find $(s,t)$, $|t| \le \epsilon |s|$ such that $s+t=1+x$ and $t$ is zero or has the same sign as $x$.
- Step 2: Let $u\approx t/s$, $w \approx yu$, $w’=0$. If $w > 0.5$ (unlikely), then:
  - Step 2a: Find $(u,u’)$, $|u’| \le \epsilon |u|$ such that $u+u’ \approx t/s$.
  - Step 2b: Find $(v,v’)$, $|v’| \le \epsilon |v|$ such that $v+v’ \approx \ln(1+u+u’)$.
  - Step 2c: Find $(w,w’)$, $|w’| \le \epsilon |w|$ such that $w+w’\approx y(v+v’)$.
- Step 3: Evaluate $(1+x)^y$ by `pow(s,y)*exp(w)*exp(w’)`.

We proceed to elaborate the steps.

**Step 1**. Construct $s+t=1+x$ by

$$
\begin{align*}
s &:=\begin{cases}
\mathrm{RU}(1+x) & \textrm{if } -1 < x < 0 \\
\mathrm{RD}(1+x) & \textrm{if } x \ge 0
\end{cases} \\
t &:=(1+x)-s
\end{align*}
$$

Then (1) $t$ is representable as a floating point number (i.e. $1+x=s+t$ exactly), (2) $s$ is finite and $s \ge 0.5 \epsilon > 0$, and (3) $|t| \le \epsilon s$.

<details>

(1) We note that for $x > -1$, the prescribed rounding for $s$ is equivalent to “proper truncating” of [De71] (Definition 3.5), i.e. one where the rounding error is either zero or has the opposite sign as the adder of smaller magnitude. This can be verified by considering the three cases: $-1 < x < 0$, $0 \ge x < 1$, and $x \ge 1$, respectively. 

Thus, it follows from Theorem 4.10 of [De71] that $1+x=s+t$ can be constructed exactly by a variant of the `Fast2Sum` algorithm, where the first (addition) step is properly truncating and the remaining two (subtraction) steps are rounded to nearest.

(2) For finite floating point value $x$, $(1+x)$ clearly cannot overflow, so $s$ is finite.

For $-1 < x < 0$,  the smallest floating point value $x$ can take is $-1+0.5\epsilon$; therefore $s = \mathrm{RU}(1+x) \ge 1+x \ge 0.5\epsilon$. And for $x \ge 0$, $s = \mathrm{RD}(1+x)  \ge 1 \ge 0.5\epsilon$. That $s \ge 0.5\epsilon$ implies $s$ is normalized.

(3)  Because the prescribed rounding of $s$ is “faithful”, i.e. there is no floating point number between $s$ and $(1+x)$, and because $t$ is equal to (minus) the rounding error, the magnitude of $t$ is less than one ULP around $s$. Since $s$ is normalized, one ULP around $s$ has relative error no larger than $\epsilon$. This shows $|t| \le \epsilon s$.

</details>

Since $s+t =1+x$ exactly, no precision is lost by rewriting $(1+x)^y$ as $s^y (1+t/s)^y$.

The purpose of the prescribed rounding for $s$, instead of rounding to nearest, is to avoid spurious underflow and overflow. That is, if $s^y$ and/or $(1+t/s)^y$ overflows (underflows), then  $(1+x)^y$ necessarily overflows (underflows). (And under no circumstance will one term underflow while the other overflows.)

<details>

Let $u \equiv t/s$. First consider $-1 < x < 0$. In this case, $0 < s \le 1$, $t \le 0$, $-\epsilon < u \le 0$, and $0 < 1+u \le 1$. If $y \ge 0$, then $s^y \le 1$ and $(1+u)^y \le 1$. Both terms are free of overflow, and if any of them underflows, their product necessarily underflows. If $y < 0$, then  $s^y \ge 1$ and $(1+u)^y \ge 1$. Both terms are free of underflow, and if any of them overflows, their product necessarily overflows.

Next, consider $x \ge 0$. In this case, $s \ge 1$, $t \ge 0$, $u \ge 0$, and $1+u \ge 1$. If $y < 0$, then $s^y \le 1$ and $(1+u)^y \le 1$. Both terms are free of overflow, and if any of them underflows, their product necessarily underflows. If $y \ge 0$, then  $s^y \ge 1$ and $(1+u)^y \ge 1$. Both terms are free of underflow, and if any of them overflows, their product necessarily overflows.

An example where the standard `Fast2Sum` algorithm (with round-to-nearest addition) is bad is `x = 1e-16`. In this case, `s = 0.9999999999999999` if rounded to nearest, and `t = 1.1022302462515656e-17`. If `y = 7e18`, then $s^y$ underflows to zero and so does the product; while the correct result is `9.86e-305`. And if `y = 1e20`, then $s^y$ underflows to zero and $(1+t/s)^y$ overflows, and their product is `nan`; the correct result is `0` (underflow).

</details>

*Remark*. This algorithm is not intended to be *correctly rounded*. There may be inputs for which the result produced by this algorithm overflows or underflows while the correctly rounded result doesn’t. However, for these inputs, the algorithm is expected to produce a result a few epsilon away from the correctly rounded result if the exponent is unbounded.

Reference issue
Toward gh-21404.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Adds a function `scipy.special.pow1p(x,y)` that computes `(1+x)**y` for real `x` and `y` for accurately than the direct formula.

It conforms to the IEEE-754 spec of the `pow` function except that (the `special` equivalent of) floating point exceptions may not be raised.

#### Additional information
Support for complex `x` and `y` may be added by a separate PR in the future.

#### Reference

[De71] Dekker, T. J. (1971) “A floating-point technique for extending the available precision.” _Numerische Mathematik_, 18:224–242.

[Mu16] Muller, J. M. (2016) Elementary Functions: Algorithms and Implementation. Birkhauser.

[Mu18] Muller, J. M. *et al* (2018) Handbook of Floating-Point Arithmetic. Birkhauser.

#### Notations and assumptions

We assume floating point numbers are representable as $`\pm d_0.d_1 d_2 \cdots d_{p-1} \times 2^e `$, where $d_i \in \\{0,1\\}$, $e_\min \le e \le e_\max$, $e_\min=1-e_\max$. The “weight” of $d_i$ is $2^{-i}$. A *normalized* number has $d_0=1$. A *subnormal* number has $d_0=0$ and $e=e_\min$. Let $\epsilon := 2^{-p+1}$ denote the *machine epsilon*. Let $\lambda:=2^{e_\min}$ denote the smallest normalized number. The smallest subnormal number is $\lambda \epsilon$.

<details>

For `binary64` type, $p=53$, $e_\min=-1022$, $e_\max=1023$, $\epsilon=2^{-52}\approx 2.22\times 10^{-16}$.

</details>

Let $\mathrm{RU}(\cdot)$ denote round toward $+\infty$, $\mathrm{RD}(\cdot)$ denote round toward $-\infty$, and $\mathrm{RN}(\cdot)$ denote round to nearest with ties resolved in any way. If $\mathrm{RN}(x)$ is normalized, then $|x-\mathrm{RN(x)}| \le 0.5\epsilon |x|$, and $|x-\mathrm{RN(x)}| \le 0.5\epsilon |\mathrm{RN}(x)|$.

Let $z \in \mathbb{R}$, $|z| < 1$. Then the following simple bounds hold:

(1) $\ln(1+z)=z(1+\delta)$ for some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\delta| \le (|z|/2)/(1-|z|)$.

(2) $\ln(1+z)=(z-z^2/2)(1+\delta)$ for some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\delta| \le (|z|^2/3)/(1-|z|/2)^2$.

(3) $e^{z}-1 = z(1+\delta)$ some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\delta| \le (|z|/2)/(1-|z|)$.

<details>

*Proof*. (1) and (2) follow from the Taylor series $\ln(1+z)=z-z^2 /2+  z^3/3 - z^4/4 + \cdots$ for $|z| < 1$. For (1), we have $|\ln(1+z)-z| = | -z^2/2 +  z^3/3 -  z^4/4 + \cdots |$ $\le  |z|^2/2 +  |z|^3/2 +  |z|^4/2 + \cdots$ $=  ( |z|^2/2) /(1-|z|)$. Dividing both sides by $|z|$ yields the desired result. For (2), we have $|\ln(1+z)-(z-z^2/2)| = |  z^3/3- z^4/4+\cdots |$ $\le  |z|^3/3 + |z|^4/3+\cdots$ $=( |z^3|/3)/(1-|z|)$. Dividing both sides by $|z-z^2/2|$ and relaxing  $1/(1-|z|)$ to $1/(1-|z|/2)$ yields the desired result.

(3) follows from the Taylor series $e^z=1+z+z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24+\cdots$. We have $|(e^z-1)-z| = | z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24+\cdots | \le |z|^2/2+|z|^3/2+|z|^4/2 + \cdots = (|z|^2/2)(1-|z|)$. Dividing both sides by $|z|$ yields the desired result.

</details>

#### Preliminary analysis

The computation of $x^y$ is briefly discussed in [Mu06] (Section 13.2). Even if the standard library function `pow(x,y)`  produces an accurate result (say to 1 ULP) for *exact*  $x$ and $y$, $(1+x)$ may not be exactly representable, in which case its rounding error would be magnified $y$ times by taking the power, since $(\mathrm{d}x^y /x^y )/(\mathrm{d}x/x)=y$. This leads to severe loss of precision e.g. for $|x | < \epsilon/2$ and large $y$.

For $x > -1$, an alternative is to evaluate $(1+x)^y$ by $e^{y\ln (1+x)}$. Again, unless $y\ln(1+x)$ is exactly representable, which is unlikely,  its rounding error gets magnified by  the exponentiation, since $(\mathrm{d} e^z / e^z)/({\mathrm{d} z / z} )= z$. Fortunately, we only have to worry about $z=y\ln(1+x)$ of magnitude not too large to cause overflow or underflow in the first place; this greatly restricts the range of interesting $z$ to $(e_\min-p) \ln 2 < z < (e_\max+1)\ln 2$. 

<details>

Overflow starts from $(2-\epsilon/2)\times 2^{e_\max}$; therefore the absence of overflow means $e^z < (2-\epsilon/2)\times 2^{e_\max} < 2^{e_\max+1}$, which implies $z < (e_\max+1) \ln 2 < 0.7(e_\max+1)$. A similar analysis shows $z > 0.7(e_\min-p)$ if $e^z$ does not underflow to zero.

For `binary64`, this means the relative error in the exponent is magnified by no more than 717 or -753 times. This magnification factor is much lower than that of the direct formula.

</details>

One way to compensate for the error magnification is to compute the exponent with higher precision. For example, if an extended precision type with $\log_2[(p-e_\min)\ln2]$ additional bits of significand is available, then we can accurately evaluate $(1+x)^y$ by `exp(y*log1p(x))` in the extended precision.

In the remaining, we describe an algorithm  to evaluate $(1+x)^y$ accurately when no extended precision data type is available.

#### Algorithm

*To be completed*

After handling the special cases as prescribed by IEEE-754, we are left with finite (floating-point numbers) $x$ and $y$ that fall into two cases:

1. $x >-1$, $y \in \mathbb{R}$;
2. $x < -1$, $y \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Let’s first examine the case $x >-1$, $y \in \mathbb{R}$, which is probably more common. The key idea is to write 

$$
(1+x)^y = s^y (1+t/s)^y = s^y e^{y \ln(1+t/s)}
$$

for some $|t| \ll |s|$, and evaluate each power accurately. The algorithm is outlined below:

- Step 1: Find $(s,t)$, $|t| \le \epsilon |s|$ such that $s+t=1+x$ and $t$ is zero or has the same sign as $x$.
- Step 2: Let $u\approx t/s$, $w \approx yu$, $w’=0$. If $w > 0.5$ (unlikely), then:
  - Step 2a: Find $(u,u’)$, $|u’| \le \epsilon |u|$ such that $u+u’ \approx t/s$.
  - Step 2b: Find $(v,v’)$, $|v’| \le \epsilon |v|$ such that $v+v’ \approx \ln(1+u+u’)$.
  - Step 2c: Find $(w,w’)$, $|w’| \le \epsilon |w|$ such that $w+w’\approx y(v+v’)$.
- Step 3: Evaluate $(1+x)^y$ by `pow(s,y)*exp(w)*exp(w’)`.

We proceed to elaborate the steps.

**Step 1**. Construct $s+t=1+x$ by

$$
\begin{align*}
s &:=\begin{cases}
\mathrm{RU}(1+x) & \textrm{if } -1 < x < 0 \\
\mathrm{RD}(1+x) & \textrm{if } x \ge 0
\end{cases} \\
t &:=(1+x)-s
\end{align*}
$$

Then (1) $t$ is representable as a floating point number (i.e. $1+x=s+t$ exactly), (2) $s$ is finite and $s \ge 0.5 \epsilon > 0$, and (3) $|t| \le \epsilon s$.

<details>

(1) We note that for $x > -1$, the prescribed rounding for $s$ is equivalent to “proper truncating” of [De71] (Definition 3.5), i.e. one where the rounding error is either zero or has the opposite sign as the adder of smaller magnitude. This can be verified by considering the three cases: $-1 < x < 0$, $0 \ge x < 1$, and $x \ge 1$, respectively. 

Thus, it follows from Theorem 4.10 of [De71] that $1+x=s+t$ can be constructed exactly by a variant of the `Fast2Sum` algorithm, where the first (addition) step is properly truncating and the remaining two (subtraction) steps are rounded to nearest.

(2) For finite floating point value $x$, $(1+x)$ clearly cannot overflow, so $s$ is finite.

For $-1 < x < 0$,  the smallest floating point value $x$ can take is $-1+0.5\epsilon$; therefore $s = \mathrm{RU}(1+x) \ge 1+x \ge 0.5\epsilon$. And for $x \ge 0$, $s = \mathrm{RD}(1+x)  \ge 1 \ge 0.5\epsilon$. That $s \ge 0.5\epsilon$ implies $s$ is normalized.

(3)  Because the prescribed rounding of $s$ is “faithful”, i.e. there is no floating point number between $s$ and $(1+x)$, and because $t$ is equal to (minus) the rounding error, the magnitude of $t$ is less than one ULP around $s$. Since $s$ is normalized, one ULP around $s$ has relative error no larger than $\epsilon$. This shows $|t| \le \epsilon s$.

</details>

Since $s+t =1+x$ exactly, no precision is lost by rewriting $(1+x)^y$ as $s^y (1+t/s)^y$.

The purpose of the prescribed rounding for $s$, instead of rounding to nearest, is to avoid spurious underflow and overflow. That is, if $s^y$ and/or $(1+t/s)^y$ overflows (underflows), then  $(1+x)^y$ necessarily overflows (underflows). (And under no circumstance will one term underflow while the other overflows.)

<details>

Let $u \equiv t/s$. First consider $-1 < x < 0$. In this case, $0 < s \le 1$, $t \le 0$, $-\epsilon < u \le 0$, and $0 < 1+u \le 1$. If $y \ge 0$, then $s^y \le 1$ and $(1+u)^y \le 1$. Both terms are free of overflow, and if any of them underflows, their product necessarily underflows. If $y < 0$, then  $s^y \ge 1$ and $(1+u)^y \ge 1$. Both terms are free of underflow, and if any of them overflows, their product necessarily overflows.

Next, consider $x \ge 0$. In this case, $s \ge 1$, $t \ge 0$, $u \ge 0$, and $1+u \ge 1$. If $y < 0$, then $s^y \le 1$ and $(1+u)^y \le 1$. Both terms are free of overflow, and if any of them underflows, their product necessarily underflows. If $y \ge 0$, then  $s^y \ge 1$ and $(1+u)^y \ge 1$. Both terms are free of underflow, and if any of them overflows, their product necessarily overflows.

An example where the standard `Fast2Sum` algorithm (with round-to-nearest addition) is bad is `x = 1e-16`. In this case, `s = 0.9999999999999999` if rounded to nearest, and `t = 1.1022302462515656e-17`. If `y = 7e18`, then $s^y$ underflows to zero and so does the product; while the correct result is `9.86e-305`. And if `y = 1e20`, then $s^y$ underflows to zero and $(1+t/s)^y$ overflows, and their product is `nan`; the correct result is `0` (underflow).

</details>

*Remark*. This algorithm is not intended to be *correctly rounded*. There may be inputs for which the result produced by this algorithm overflows or underflows while the correctly rounded result doesn’t. However, for these inputs, the algorithm is expected to produce a result a few epsilon away from the correctly rounded result if the exponent is unbounded.

**Step 2**. This step is needed only if $t \ne 0$ and $s^y$ does not underflow to zero or overflow to infinity.

Write $(1+t/s)^y = e^{y \ln(1+t/s)}$. Let 

$$
\begin{align*}
u &:= \mathrm{RN}(t/s) \\
w &:= \mathrm{RN}(yu) \\
\end{align*}
$$

where $\mathrm{RN}(\cdot)$ denotes round to nearest. Then $|y\ln(1+t/s)-w| \le (2|w|+1)\epsilon$.

<details>

From the Taylor series $\ln(1+z)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}z^k/k$ for $|z| < 1$, we find $|\ln(1+z)-z| = | \sum_{k=2}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}z^k/k | \le \sum_{k=2}^\infty \frac12 |z|^k= \frac12 |z|^2 /(1-|z|)$. This can be rewritten as $\ln(1+z)=z(1+\delta_0)$ where $|\delta_0| \le 0.5|z|/(1-|z|)$. Substituting $z=t/s$ yields $\ln(1+t/s)=(t/s)(1+\delta_0)$ where $|\delta_0| \le 0.5 |t/s|/(1-|t/s|) \le 0.5\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$, since $|t/s| \le \epsilon$.

Using a standard result that $x=\mathrm{RN}(x)(1+\delta)+\eta$ for some $|\delta|\le 0.5\epsilon$ and some $\eta \le \lambda\epsilon$, we can write $t/s=u(1+\delta_1)+\eta_1$, $|\delta_1| \le 0.5\epsilon$, $|\eta_1|\le \lambda\epsilon$, and $yu=w(1+\delta_2)+\eta_2$, $|\delta_2| \le 0.5 \epsilon$, $|\eta_2|\le \lambda \epsilon$.

Putting these together, we can write  $y\ln(1+t/s)=y(t/s)(1+\delta_0)$ $`=y[u(1+\delta_1)+\eta_1](1+\delta_0)`$ $`=(yu)(1+\delta_1)(1+\delta_0)+y\eta_1(1+\delta_0)`$ $`=[w(1+\delta_2)+\eta_2](1+\delta_1)(1+\delta_0)+y\eta_1(1+\delta_0)`$. Ignoring higher order terms, the absolute error is $`|y\ln(1+t/s)-w| \approx |w(\delta_2+\delta_1+\delta_0)+\eta_2+y\eta_1|`$. Note that $`|y\eta_1| \le 2^{e_\max+1} 2^{e_\min-p+1}=\epsilon$. Then the absolute is (first-order) bounded by $(2|w|+1)\epsilon$.

</details>

Since the relative error of $\exp(z)$ is equal to the absolute error of $z$ (assuming $\exp$ itself is exact), this implies the relative error of $(1+t/s)^y$ is bounded by $2\epsilon$ if $|w| \le 0.5$. The error is much lower for moderate (and probably common) values of $y$.

If $|w| > 0.5$ and especially $|w| \gg 1$, the rounding error in $w$ may be magnified (by hundreds of times). However, provided that $s^y$ does not underflow to zero or overflow, this can only happen for small $x$ and large $y$; specifically, $|w| > 0.5$ implies $|x| < 1$ and $|y| > 0.5\epsilon^{-1}$.

<details>

Since $|u| \approx |t/s| \le \epsilon$ and $|w| \approx |yu| > 0.5$, we find $|y| > 0.5 \epsilon^{-1} = 2^{p-2}$.

The condition that `pow(s,y)` remains positive and finite means $2^{e_\min-p} < s^y < 2^{e_\max+1}$. Taking 2-based logarithm and using the assumption that $(p-e_\min) > (e_\max+1)$ yields $|y\log_2s| < p-e_\min$. It follows that $|log_2s| < (p-e_\min) \times 2^{2-p}$. For practical floating point formats, the right-hand side is very close to $0$, and definitely less than one. This shows $s < 2$, and hence $x < 1$.

</details>

We proceed to improve the accuracy for $|x| < 1$ and $|y| > 0.5\epsilon^{-1}$. Rounding error may be introduced in three places: (a) the division `t/s`, (b) the `log1p` call, and (c) the multiplication `y*log1p`. To reduce the rounding error, we perform the three steps using essentially double-word arithmetic.

<details>

Numerical examples could be constructed where rounding error from any one of the three operations gets magnified in the final result, even if the other two operations, as well as `exp`, are computed to infinite precision.

(1) Let `x = -0.0001`, `y = 2e19`. Then `s = 0.9999`, `t = -1.1018204577883939e-17`. The relative error of $t \oslash s$ is around `5e-17`. Even if the succeeding steps are computed to infinite precision, the relative error of the final result is around `1e-14`.

(2) Let `x = -5e-17`, `y = 9e18`. Then `s = 1` and `t = -5e-17` exactly. `log1p(-5e-17) = -5e-17`; its relative error is around `-2.5e-17`. Even if the succeeding steps are computed to infinite precision, the relative error of the final result is around `1.1e-14`.

</details>

Then (1) $r$ is representable as a floating point number (i.e. $t=us+r$ exactly), (2) $r/s=t/s-u$, (3) $|u'| \le 0.5\epsilon(1+0.5 \epsilon)|u| \le \epsilon |u|$, and (4) $|(t/s)-(u+u’)| \le 0.25\epsilon^2 |t/s|$.

Dividing both sides by $|z-0.5z^2|$ yields $\ln(1+z)=(z-0.5z^2)(1+\delta)$ where $|\delta| \le (1/3) |z|^2/(1-|z|)^2$. Let’s now examine the case $x <-1$, $y \in \mathbb{Z}$. Let $x' := -x$. Then $x' > 1$, $(1+x)^y = (-1)^y (x'-1)^y$. We proceed to evaluate $(x'-1)^y$.

For $1 < x' \le 2^p$, it is easy to verify that $(x'-1)$ is representable as a floating point number. Therefore, for this range of $x'$, we simply call `pow(1+x, y)`.

For $2^p < x' \le 2^{2p}$, which are all even integers, $(x'-1)$ is not representable as a floating point number. However, we may construct floating point numbers $s := \mathrm{RD}(x'-1)$, $t:=(x'-1)-s$. They satisfy $t/s \le \epsilon$. We can then compute $(x'-1)^y = s^y (1+t/s)^y$ like before. The direct formula `pow(1+x,y)` gives `-1.7976931348623135e+308`, which has a relative error of `-1.1e-15` compared to a correctly rounded result produced by `mpmath`. The decomposition method gives `-1.7976931348623155e+308`, which is equal to the correctly rounded result.

If $x > 2^{2p}$, an exact decomposition like the above is not possible. However, recall that $(\mathrm{d}x^y / x^y) = y (\mathrm d x/x)$. For very large $x'$, the relative error of representing $x'-1$ by $x'$ is small, and the range of $y$ that does not lead to overflow or underflow is also small. Therefore their product, which is equal to the relative error of the result, is also small. Specifically, it can be shown that for such $x'$ and $y$, $|(x'-1)^y - (x')^y| \le \epsilon|(x'-1)^y|$. This allows us to simply evaluate $(x'-1)^y$ by `pow(x', y)` (which is the same as `pow(x'-1, y)`).

*Proof*. The condition that $(x'-1)^y$ does not overflow or underflow to zero implies $2^{e_\min-p} < (x'-1)^y < 2^{e_\max+1}$. Taking 2-based logarithm and dividing both sides by $\log_2(x'-1)$ yields $(e_\min-p)/\log_2(x'-1) < y < (e_\max+1)/\log_2(x'-1)$. Because $x' > 2^{2p}$ is an integer, $x'-1 \ge 2^{2p}$. This allows the inequality to be relaxed into the simpler form $(e_\min-p)/(2p) < y < (e_\max+1)/(2p)$.
